#3514. GTA 6 Is Apparently Everything Rockstar Promised And Then Some

At long last, Grand Theft Auto 6 launch day has come. With Rockstar's latest project steadily unlocking as the clock strikes midnight worldwide, GTA 6 reviews have gone live, and the praise has been overwhelmingly positive so far. In fact, GTA 6 is reviewing so well that it's currently tied with the 1998 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game of all time on GameSpot's sister site Metacritic, a feat that has taken 28 years to equal.

So what are the reviewers saying? Amongst the flurry of perfect scores, a lot of the consensus is geared toward the world that Rockstar Games has created for its co-protagonists to inhabit, a sandbox that reacts to you in a variety of unique and interesting ways. It's a genre-defining experience for open-world games, as Rockstar has raised the bar to a tremendously high level for any other open-world game that'll follow in its footsteps.

Here's what some reviewers have to say, and for more on the game, check out GameSpot's GTA 6 guides hub for an evolving collection of walkthroughs, tips, and tricks.

Grand Theft Auto 6

  • Platforms: PS5 and Xbox Series X|S
  • Price $80 for the Standard Edition, $100 for the Ultimate Edition
  • Release date: November 19

GameSpot -- 10/10

Only Rockstar commands the time and money necessary to make a game as dedicated to small details. And only Rockstar can execute on the realizing such a granular vision unimpeachably. The obsession with the minutia both explains and justifies the 13-year wait. This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA 6 is an astonishing open-world action game that I’d wager won’t be outdone until Grand Theft Auto 7.  -- Tamoor Hussain [Full review]

IGN -- 100

Exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played. -- Luke Reilly [Full review]

The Guardian -- 5/5

With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, over the top chaos--as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its center -- Keza MacDonald [Full review]

Destructoid -- 10/10

Grand Theft Auto 6 is part criminal come-up tale, part love story, and part life sim all wrapped up in an impossibly deep and detailed Rockstar Games open world that may never run out of things to do. For the last three-plus weeks, I have been gleefully vacationing in Vice City: robbing banks, fighting drug dealers, stealing cars, and enjoying the view while not coming close to finishing everything it has to offer. GTA 6 is finally here now, and it was well worth the wait. -- Scott Duwe [Full review]

Eurogamer -- 5/5

A game of opposites and awe, minute detail and impossible scale, Rockstar pushes back the horizon of video games once again with GTA 6. An irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action - and a load more after that. -- Chris Tapsell [Full review]

Bloomberg -- 5/5

It turns out that the secret ingredients to a great game are a lot of money, time and talented people. -- Jason Schreier [Full review]

Game Informer -- 10/10

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a generational game that stands toe-to-toe with many of the great crime stories and satires across other media. It showcases both the entertainment value of interactive play and the current high-water mark for technical and artistic detail in games. Hunt for and count up all the minor faults or foibles you like, but then note how you just spent another hour lost in this remarkable escape into criminality, wanton violence, egregious sex, and the elusive potential of true love. -- Matt Miller [Full review]

SiliconEra -- 90/100

Rockstar made strides in incorporating all the systems and the open world into the campaign in a satisfying way. But Jason and Lucia are the glue that keeps everything together. It’s their chemistry and complicity that made me want to experience everything, and it’s them that will keep me coming back. -- Daniel Bueno [Full review]

Screenhub -- 4/5

At its core, GTA 6 is a pretty good game. There are large sections where it is an absolutely epic game, and large sections that are boring and too limited. However, after I pushed through the boring parts and it opened up enough to become a proper GTA title, it became worth it. Regardless of whether the game was good, it was always going to be an inescapable cultural moment. Luckily, it’s one largely worth participating in. -- Alice Clarke [Full review]

Kotaku -- No score

GTA 6 is a truly remarkable game. A masterpiece of open-world design that brings forward the best parts of all of Rockstar’s past games into one billion-dollar adventure that is unlike anything I’ve played before. It’s a game I’ll be playing for years, and I can’t wait to talk about it with others. -- Zack Zwiezen [Full review]

The Verge -- No score

It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA 6is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it. -- Andrew Webster [Full review]

#3512. GTA 6 Isn’t Worth Buying A Fancy Controller For

In all the excitement surrounding Grand Theft Auto VI (check out our 10/10 review), it might be tempting to upgrade your setup. For a game 13 years in the making, is now the time to upgrade my TV? Maybe a PS5 Pro is in order? It's a coincidence I finally upgraded my speaker system after 18 years, I swear.

One cheaper upgrade than those above you might be considering is a better controller, like a DualSense Edge or Xbox Elite controller. For all of their myriad upgrades, the most essential reason to ever buy one of these, in my opinion, is for the back paddles. Although they are not technically extra buttons, the ability to map an inconveniently placed button to one of them can make an experience far smoother. 

Some games make an exceptionally strong case for only playing with paddles. You do a lot of sprinting and picking things up in Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, and having to take my thumb off the right stick (thus temporarily locking the camera in place) is something I find to be a constant annoyance. It's such an improvement to be able to do those things while keeping my thumbs where they belong.

Grand Theft Auto VI, on the other hand, is not such an example. Rockstar has finally made a change to the default control scheme it uses in its games, mapping sprint to a click of the left stick, rather than the traditional usage of the X (PlayStation) and A (Xbox) buttons. That alone alleviates a potential argument for needing back paddles (at least as much as one can need such a thing).

That's not to say there's literally zero use for one of these pro-style controllers in GTA 6. In our experience, tapping a paddle is arguably still an improvement to clicking the left stick to sprint or holding L1/LB to bring up the weapon wheel. Enabling Focus Mode is done by clicking both sticks, which you might find awkward; accomplishing that with paddles might be comfortable for you.

GTA 6 doesn't allow its controls to be freely remapped, though there are some options available (such as reverting to that previous style of sprinting). So while there are some reasons you may want to set up the paddles of your pro controller before diving into GTA, it's safe to say that buying one just for this game ain't worth it.

#3511. Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond

It looks like Robert Pattinson is trading in his Batmobile for an Aston Martin. After a highly scrutinized and lengthy audition process involving some of Hollywood’s most sought-after leading men, it was the Batman star who emerged at the eleventh hour to nab the role of MI6 agent James Bond.

“James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” said Pattinson in a statement. “I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya, and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Created by Ian Fleming for his 1953 novel Casino Royale, James Bond, the British intelligence officer who lends his immense talents to MI6, is one of the most recognizable characters in the modern world. Figuring prominently in 12 of Fleming’s novels and two collections of short stories, Bond is both tall, dark, and handsome and calm, cool, and collected—the platonic ideal of a world-class spy. Bond leapt from page to screen in 1962 with the Eon-produced Dr. No, spawning one of the biggest media franchises in history. Since its inception, the 27 Bond films have grossed more than $7 billion dollars worldwide.

Pattinson follows in the suave footsteps of Daniel Craig, who played James Bond for five films, from 2006’s Casino Royale until 2021’s No Time to Die where (spoiler alert) Craig’s 007 dies while protecting the world from a global terrorist organization. Around No Time to Die, there was another shake up in Bond ownership when Amazon acquired Bond’s parent studio, MGM, in an $8.5 billion deal. Barbara Broccoli—whose father, Eon founder Albert R. “Cubby” Broccoli, produced the first Bond film—and her half brother, Michael G. Wilson, held the rights to the franchise for almost 30 years, and pledged to work with Amazon. However, in February 2025, Broccoli and Wilson announced that they’d be stepping back from the franchise and ceding complete creative control to Amazon MGM. At the Oscars a month later, the Broccoli family was honored with a bizarre musical tribute to James Bond, starring Margaret Qualley, Doja Cat, and Lisa, unofficially ushering in a new era in the Bond Cinematic Universe.

Although a new era of Bond loomed, Amazon MGM had one major problem: They needed a new Bond. Ahead of No Time to Die, Craig had announced that he was stepping away from the franchise, leaving the producers with a 007-sized hole to fill. Before she stepped away, Broccoli insinuated that this new era of Bond was looking for a younger actor, in their 30s, to take over the reins from Craig, who was 51 when he retired from MI6.

Technically, they landed on someone slightly outside their preferred age range; Pattinson is 40 years old. Just don’t tell him that. During Vanity Fair’s lie detector test with Jennifer Lawrence while promoting their film Die My Love, Pattinson insisted he was from a different generation. I am Gen Z,” he said to Lawrence. “I am.” Hey, you’re only as old as you feel. In the same video, Pattinson said he “likes taking jobs of younger actors,” which he managed to do with his Bond casting. Good for Pattinson.

Almost every leading man in Hollywood’s name came up as a potential predecessor to Craig—except for Pattinson, who the masses assumed was out of contention due to the fact that he locked into playing another beloved fictional character with massive IP: Batman. Pattinson’s take on the caped crusader in Matt Reeve’s The Batman (2022) was a major success, but several production delays on The Batman Part II, and a shakeup at Batman’s studio, DC—last week, it was announced that the co-CEOs of DC Productions, James Gunn and Peter Safran, were ousted from the studio—meant that there might be time in Pattinson’s schedule for some sexy espionage.

Still, it was far from a done deal that Pattinson would land 007. In recent years, some fans have advocated for a twist on the classic Bond formula. Lashana Lynch made history as Nomi, the first Black person to ever to hold the 007 moniker, in No Time to Die. But Nomi is not James Bond. There was a seemingly endless period when the world was convinced that Idris Elba—arguably the most tall, dark, and handsome man to ever exist—would take on the mantle at some point, but it wasn’t meant to be. Now, at 53, Elba has seemingly aged out of the role. (For the record, Elba thought the next Bond should be a woman.) Elba wasn’t the only name bandied about in recent years. It was reported in 2024 that Aaron Taylor-Johnson was close to signing a contract to take over the role, but those reports were never confirmed.

Although a favorite at the beginning, Jacob Elordi reportedly didn’t screen test for the role. Riz Ahmed made an Emmy-nominated television show, Bait, inspired by the idea of a British Pakistani actor getting cast as Bond. Other actors rumored to be in the mix over the course of the process include, but are not limited to, Tom Francis, Harris Dickinson, and, apparently, Harry Styles. At the end of the day, five actors reportedly screen-tested for the role: Slow Horse’s Jack Lowden, One Night Only’s Callum Turner, Disclosure Day’s Josh O’Connor, Superman’s Nicholas Hoult, and Pattison. Hoult and Pattinson were the last names to emerge as contenders for the role, implying that the powers that be at Amazon MGM may not have been happy with the three options presented and sent a hail mary. When Puck reported that Pattinson was able to negotiate a three-picture deal rather than a four-picture deal despite commanding a much higher salary than the other options, it looked like the writing was on the wall that Pattinson would be the next Bond.

It also helps that Pattinson is having a career high at the moment, having starred in a handful of the most critically acclaimed and commercially successful films of 2026. He began the year by turning his controversial A24 comedy The Drama with Zendaya into a box-office success, generating $134 million worldwide on a reported budget of about $28 million. He then followed that up with a deliciously sniveling turn in Christopher Nolan’s epic The Odyssey, an Oscar front-runner that earned $1.8 billion at the box office. Then there’s Primetime, the Lance Oppenheim drama starring Pattinson as To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen. (Yes, in a way, Chris Hansen is now one degree from being James Bond. Let that sink in). Primetime hit big with $62 million globally on an $14.5 million budget, and is earning Pattinson leading-actor buzz. On top of it all, he’s still got Dune: Part Three with Denis Villeneuve coming down the pipeline in December.

Ultimately, the Twilight star was handpicked by the powers that be at Amazon MGM, including producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman and director Denis Villeneuve, who is helming the next iteration of the series based on a script from screenwriter Steven Knight, with Tanya Lapointe executive producing. Given the fact that Pattinson is starring in Villeneuve’s highly-anticipated Dune: Part Three, it might not be that much of a surprise that the director chose Pattinson as his next Bond. “Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey,” said Villeneuve in a statement. “We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007. I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.”

Pattinson enters a long lineage of spectacularly suave spies—some who lasted longer than others in Bond’s impeccably tailored suits. The first-ever James Bond was, of course, Sean Connery, who went on to star in six Bond films, including From Russia With Love (1963), Goldfinger (1964), and Diamonds Are Forever (1971). Connery was followed by George Lazenby, who starred in a single Bond film, On Her Majesty’s Secret Service (1969), before passing the reins back to Connery. The third Bond was Roger Moore, who took over for 1973’s Live and Let Die, and appeared in a total of seven Bond films, most notably The Spy Who Loved Me (1977) and Octopussy (1983).

After Moore came Timothy Dalton, who became 007 with 1987’s The Living Daylights, then threw in the towel after 1989’s License to Kill. Millennials will fondly remember the next Bond: Pierce Brosnan, who starred as the sexy spy in four films from 1995’s GoldenEye to 2002’s Die Another Day, until Craig took over in 2006.

Will Pattison’s Bond be more debonair like Brosnan, who told VF he was “eagerly” awaiting the Bond casting news, or brooding like Craig? Will he be remembered as a rightful heir to Connery’s throne, or will his Bond feel closer to Austin Powers in The Spy Who Shagged Me? In any case, let’s hope Pattinson prefers his martinis shaken not stirred. He’s going to be drinking a lot of them for the foreseeable future.

There are few things I love more than a reality show, and after years of devouring The Traitors with my Peacock subscription, I was thrilled to hear that the folks behind that Emmy-winning series were creating another. Enter The Mob, another campy competition show that's available in its entirety with a Hulu subscription. The show once again proved that RuPaul's Drag Race alum Willam Belli is a top-tier TV personality, but it turns out that not even the cast knew the rules when cameras went up.

The Mob's jobs feel more urgent than The Traitors' missions, but it took some adjusting to its format. Even the cast had a hard time with this, mostly because they didn't actually know all of the rules of the show they were competing on. During a recent clip from Gayety's Instagram, Willam spoke about her experience shooting the series, saying:

I asked for the rules every episode and I didn't get them until Episode 4, a printed copy. We did not know what was going on and we really wanted to. But information is power, and I understand that you don't want a reality show contestant to have power. So keeping them in dark leads to better stakes for the game and I understand that now.

Well, my mind is blown. It was hard enough to nail down the rules and format of The Mob as a viewer, but the fact that the cast was similarly clueless is truly wild to me. It didn't make the show's first four episodes any less entertaining, even though many of my favorite contestants got whacked way too early. Still, I'd think that the powers that be on production would want the reality TV personalities to at least know everything about the game they were expected to play.

As much as I enjoyed the first season of The Mob, I have to assume that the gameplay might have been even more dynamic if the cast knew the show's rules from the jump. Indeed, the first few eliminations were a little sleepy, such as Dancing with the Stars judge Bruno Tonioli pledging allegiance to Joe Gorga and then immediately getting whacked.

You can see Willam Belli's comments about The Mob and feeling a bit clueless at the start of filming below:

Willam might be the only contestant from RuPaul's Drag Race to get disqualified, but that doesn't mean she went against the rules in every situation. After all, The Mob cast were starting a brand new competition series, and didn't have any previous episodes to use as a reference. The folks who caught on seemed to make it the farthest, but it was curtains for other favorites like Willam, Bruno, and Debi Mazar.

The Mob is streaming in its entirety on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. We'll just have to see if it gets renewed for a second season, and how the gameplay changes with contestants who know what to expect.

#3509. GTA 6 Finally Changed The Default Rockstar-Game Controls

If you've played Rockstar series like Grand Theft Auto or Read Dead Redemption over the past few decades, then you're familiar with their default control scheme, which maps sprinting to a face button instead of the left analog stick. But Grand Theft Auto VI isn't being hailed as a revolutionary game for nothing--at long last, the default scheme has changed.

As we learned while playing Grand Theft Auto VI, instead of the default setup mapping sprint to a button (A on Xbox and X on PS5), the game maps it to the left analog stick. However, you're free to switch it back to the style used in games like Red Dead Redemption 2, if you prefer.

This is a very handy change, because mapping sprinting to a face button effectively stops you from being able to easily do some of your other actions, unless you have no dignity like me and will use your own face to press a button when your hands are full.

The new default control scheme is far from the most impressive thing in Grand Theft Auto 6, of course. The game earned a rare 10/10 in our GTA 6 review, with Tamoor Hussain calling it "the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach."

For more on the game, check out our ever-expanding GTA 6 guides hub and learn what you should do first. That shouldn't include buying a whole new pro controller, however.

#3507. McDonald’s Knows You Won’t Want To Pause GTA 6 To Make Dinner

Contrary to popular belief, you'll need some nutrients to sustain your Grand Theft Auto 6 sessions this week. That means losing valuable time whipping up a meal or driving to your nearest Cluckin' Bell, but McDonald's in the US is aiming to make refueling easier by teaming up with the instant messaging app Discord.

While the fast-food chain already offers a delivery service via its McDelivery app, you won't need to reach for your smartphone to access it. Instead, you can open the McDonald's activity in Discord--which is available on console--place a McDelivery order on Uber Eats, and go back to GTA 6 while you wait for your order to arrive. Alternatively, you can also play Fast Lane Feast, a Discord-exclusive minigame where you collect burgers and chips while racing for a spot on the leaderboards.

Wait for that knock at the door, grab your grub, stuff your food-hole, and get back to your GTA 6 session after you've washed your hands. Repeat as necessary until either the game or the fast food fills the void inside you.

As the GTA 6 week kicks off across the globe — starting in Middle-earth AKA New Zealand — it looks like multiple brands are looking to get involved in what is shaping up to be a major cultural moment for interactive entertainment. KFC is holding a fake funeral in case you want to use up some of your compassionate leave to attend it and take the day off; The Weather Channel has shared a preview of Leonida's weather system, and Xbox is doing its own thing while not explicitly mentioning GTA 6 due to the marketing deal that PlayStation has with the game.

Another big promotion tonight is with the NBA's Miami Heat, as the team will represent the game with GTA 6-inspired gear and a Vice City-themed court for their match against the Milwaukee Bucks.

#3506. Zendaya “Felt Overwhelmed” on the Set of ‘The Odyssey.’ Luckily, Tom Holland Came to Support Her

On the set of The Odyssey, in which Zendaya plays the goddess Athena, there were some particularly challenging days, as the actor recalled during a recent special screening attended by the cast at Los Angeles’s Academy Museum of Motion Pictures. While filming certain scenes—especially those with a crowd of extras—the 30-year-old actor felt “incredibly nervous,” she said.

How did she manage to keep the situation under control? Thank her husband, Tom Holland, whom Zendaya says went to set that day to cheer her up. Spider-Man: Brand New Day star Holland also appears in The Odyssey as Telemachus, son of Odysseus and Penelope. And although he wasn’t scheduled to work at that particular moment, he showed up anyway to support his wife.

Matt Damon’s Odysseus consults with Zendaya’s Athena in The Odyssey.

“I felt overwhelmed, to say the least,” Zendaya said at the screening, as reported by the Daily Mail, with the actor looking stunning in her cream-colored one-shoulder dress, pixie cut, and Christian Louboutin stilettos. “It was interesting because I was on a night shoot, and I remember I came in and I was like, This is like, a pinch-me moment…. I’m in front of these people who I’ve admired, but I’m just like, I don’t want to mess this up.”

While she admitted that these emotions might have worked for her character, they were not so good for her state of mind: “I was incredibly nervous, which I guess is helpful for the scene, but there’s so many other background actors as well who are performing their hearts out—so many—stunt performers who are performing and giving the most beautiful performances.”

The turning point came when Holland stepped behind the scenes to encourage her. “It helped that Tom came to set that day, and he was, like, in the corner like, ‘You got this, you’re doing good.’” It was a team effort.

Zendaya and Holland are one of Hollywood’s most admired couples, not only for their discretion (they quietly married last August 4 in Surrey) but also for the care with which they address sensitive issues, such as mental health. Even in the cult series Euphoria, Zendaya’s character, Rue, grapples with psychological issues—in addition to addiction—as a way to raise public awareness and combat the stigma that often surrounds these kinds of situations.

It's a wild time for the superhero genre, specifically on the DC side of things. James Gunn's departure as co-CEO of the studio broke the internet, and fans who spent years watching the DC movies in order have countless questions about what comes next. I've been especially curious about the future of The Penguin (which is streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and now we have an idea about what's going on behind the scenes.

The Penguin is a spinoff of The Batman, and became an Emmy-winning hit after it arrived on HBO. The TV series made me way more invested in Matt Reeves' franchise, and I desperately want a sophomore season to be green lit. During Deadline's recent report about where things stand at DC, it claims that The Penguin showrunner Lauren LeFranc is "in talks" to produce a Poison Ivy series. Unfortunately, the studio is focused on The Batman: Part II before it can plan any potential return to The Penguin.

The Batman: Part II is in the midst of filming, following delays and Matt Reeves' departure due to a family issue. Amidst leadership shakeups, the studio is seemingly focused on getting that title in the can. Fingers crossed that we we get more of The Penguin whenever that movie is finally completed.

The idea of Lauren LeFranc producing a Poison Ivy TV series is a thrilling one, although that developing project isn't set within the Matt Reeves Batman universe. I'll be sat if/when that show comes to life, but I also really need to see more of The Penguin, particularly Cristin Milioti's Sofia Falcone/ The Hangman.

Sofia was one of the main protagonists of The Penguin, and the actress' performance was incredible and earned her an Emmy Award. Unfortunately, Milioti won't be part of The Batman: Part II, despite her popularity among fans. What's more, Colin Farrell claimed he's only in two scenes of the forthcoming sequel. So why not put Cobblepot and Falcone center stage for a second installment of the acclaimed HBO series?

Right now there are countless questions about upcoming DC movies, and what's coming next for the burgeoning DC Universe. We're currently only a few installments into the original plans for Gunn's first slate of projects, titled Gods and Monsters. His replacement Jeremy Latcham is expected to start his run as the new CEO of the studio on December 1st, so maybe we'll get more information then.

As of now, The Batman: Part II is expected to arrive in theaters on February 18th, 2028. If we have to wait that long before getting more news about The Penguin's future, fans like me are going to have to continue practicing patience. Give us more of Sofia Falcone, you cowards!

#3504. ‘NCIS: Origins’ Stars Share What Dead [Spoiler]'s Cameo Means and What's Next

NCIS: Origins is blurring the lines between past and present — but will they fully ignore the NCIS cannon and bring certain characters back to life?

Warning: Spoilers below from season 3, episode 6, of NCIS: Origins.

During the Tuesday, November 17, episode of the hit CBS series, present-day Leroy Jethro Gibbs (Mark Harmon) passed out in his basement after his prior gunshot wound seemingly got infected.

While unconscious, Gibbs slipped in and out of a dream state — jumping from the ‘90s, where he spoke with Lala Dominguez (Mariel Molino), and to a full fantasy where he came face-to-face with a grown-up version of his former boss Mike Franks (Muse Watson), who died during season 8 of NCIS. (Watson played Franks on the flagship series on and off from 2006 to 2011 before his character’s death. He made cameos from seasons 9 to 15, which spanned from 2012 to 2017.)

Watson’s cameo as Franks had some fans wondering whether Origins writers would forgo the NCIS cannon and he could actually be alive in an alternate universe. The cast, however, exclusively told Us that was never a real option.

“That one, I didn’t [believe was possible], as much as I can hope,” Kyle Schmid, who plays the younger Franks that runs the show in the ‘90s, exclusively told Us.

Schmid, 42, revealed that even without older Franks being alive in any universe, the character could continue to pop up — in another dream sequence or fever dream.

“What I do think the show does very well is utilizes the fact that they can bring Muse back in any capacity as a figment of Gibbs’ mind,” Schmid explained. “So now that that door is open, I want to see more of Muse on the show as often as I can.”

During Tuesday’s episode, dead Franks came to Gibbs in his dream and confessed that Lala didn’t die in a plane crash like he said she did back in the ‘90s. (Fans have not seen Lala die, but older Gibbs has hinted that her off-camera death left a big hole in his life.)

“We had a funeral,” Franks told Gibbs in his hallucination. “[Is it] so hard for you to believe that Dominguez could fake her own death?”

Franks then hinted that she “had help” disappearing, which launched Gibbs back into the ‘90s and a case they called “Tropicana.” In the past case, Lala and Franks helped a woman and her child escape her abusive drug-dealing ex and they were never heard from again.

“You made Lala disappear, just like that woman and her daughter,” Gibbs told Franks, who cheekily responded, “Sounds like something we’d do, don’t it?”

Gibbs was visibly upset that his mentor had kept Lala’s fake death a secret from him, but Franks explained to him, “You remember how it was probie. She was in trouble with both sides of the law. Lala had no choice but to disappear.”

Franks further revealed that Lala didn’t tell Gibbs the truth because she knew he would’ve “ripped yourself apart trying to make things right.”

“She lied because she loved you probie and I helped because, hell, I loved you both,” he confessed.

During the final moments of the episode, Gibbs asked Franks where Lala is, but he just laughed.

“How the hell should I know? I’m just a figment of your imagination,” Franks quipped before they said their goodbyes and Gibbs woke up back in present-day, four days after he passed out.

According to Schmid, Gibbs’s conversation with his former boss is only the beginning of the search for Lala in present-day — and possible flashbacks or mirages down the line.

“If you know Gibbs as well as I do, you got a dog with a bone,” Schmid told Us of what’s to come. “We’re not going to stop anything. Gibbs certainly isn’t going to stop anything.”

The actor teased, “And as we slowly peel away the layers of that onion, there’s going to be parts that are sweet, and there’s going to be parts that are going to make you cry.”

Watson, meanwhile, told Us that another cameo from older, now dead Franks, isn’t off the table either.

“I did not realize how much I miss that,” Watson said of walking on set after a break from the NCIS universe. “There’s a lot of things about the business I don’t miss, but one of them is being right there checking the camera angle and the lighting and everything on you know, turning your face the right way, and it’s just, oh gosh, it was such a thrill.”

He revealed that in the future, “If these guys, who I love to death, need me, I’m there.”

Schmid added that “there’s purpose to everything that happens” on NCIS: Origins and the writers’ reintroduction of older Franks wasn’t a fluke.

“Franks was such a big part of Gibbs’s life that it’s almost impossible to forget or have that kind of angel on your shoulder,” he shared. “And so I can’t speak for other characters, all I can do is say that I hope we can get Muse back as often as possible.”

#3503. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 Pro (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

#3502. Glenn Close Gets Teary-Eyed as She Finally Gets Her Oscar at the Governors Awards

The day before the Governors Awards, a studio executive who had attended the past few years told me that she often found herself crying at the star-studded gala. The annual awards ceremony, held by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, is often an emotional event, with honorary Oscar statuettes bestowed on influential figures in the film industry. A tribute to Michael J. Fox in 2022 and a posthumous honor for Quincy Jones in 2024 left many guests misty-eyed.

At Sunday’s gala, that teary-eyed trend continued when Glenn Close finally got to hold her own Oscar, after eight nominations without a win. Others got emotional when Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler, the independent producers from Killer Films, were honored for their tireless work making boundary-pushing and challenging movies. And when Floyd Norman, the 91-year-old artist who was the first Black animator to join Walt Disney Animation Studios, thanked his wife and five children, the crowd cheered along with him. Even though honoree Ridley Scott couldn’t attend, he dedicated his award to his late brother Tony Scott in a video message. “It is about time we all saw him with an Academy Award in his hand,” said Matt Damon in his remarks for Scott, who has been nominated for four Oscars but has never won competitively.

The presentation of honorary Oscars is often a way to correct Academy Award history, recognizing those who have been overlooked but deserve to be honored for their lifetime of dedication to storytelling and film. The Governors Awards ceremony is also a major stop on the Oscar season campaign trail, with a room packed full of stars and filmmakers from the year’s contenders.

This year that meant a surprising number of couple contenders, including Monica Barbaro and Andrew Garfield (who both star in Artificial), Carrie Coon and Tracy Letts (The Liberation), and Zendaya and Tom Holland. Though Zendaya and Holland arrived together and walked through the Ray Dolby Ballroom as a pair, they actually sat at different tables—Zendaya at the Dune table, with Timothée Chalamet and director Denis Villeneuve, and Holland at the Odyssey table, with director Christopher Nolan. Chalamet also made a date night out of the event, bringing Kylie Jenner with him.

The room held a mix of A-list Hollywood stars, like Tom Cruise (in support of Digger), Julianne Moore (The Debut), and Charlize Theron (The Odyssey), and breakout filmmakers of the year, like Obsession’s Curry Barker, La Bola Negra’s Los Javis, and Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman.

Another breakout of the season, La Bola Negra star Guitarricadelafuente, has been busy promoting the film as both an actor and a musician, having written the original song “La Nieve.” I wondered if he was exhausted from doing double duty. “I’m not tired,” he said with a smile, raving that he had enjoyed meeting many of the other songwriters in the race this year.

All four of the presenters who handed the Oscars to the honorees are also in the Oscar race this year. Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother star Mahershala Ali honored Norman; Wild Horse Nine star John Malkovich honored his Dangerous Liaisons costar Close; Julianne Moore, teaming up with Todd Haynes, honored Vachon and Koffler; and Damon, the star of The Odyssey, honored Scott.

As Close took the stage to accept the award from Malkovich, she wiped tears away from her eyes. The star of films including Fatal Attraction, 101 Dalmatians, The Wife, Albert Nobbs, and The Big Chill spoke about being raised in a religious cult and how, in her childhood, animated films were her only escape. She also spoke about being nominated for eight Oscars over her career, insisting that it didn’t phase her not to emerge victorious. “As an outsider, I have never worried about whether I was going to win or not,” she says. “I have always felt that the great honor is to be in the room.”

She wrapped up her speech with a strong statement against AI. “The craft of acting and of great storytelling has never been more vital to the existence of our fragile, violent, but capable-of-transcendence species,” she said. “We are not machines. We are flawed. Our imperfections are our salvation.”

Vachon and Koffler have been making indie films through Killer Films since 1995, championing movies like Far From Heaven, Boys Don’t Cry, Kids, Carol, and Still Alice (which won Moore her Academy Award for lead actress). They dedicated their awards to the many people they’d worked with over the years, some of whom were in the room. “We have walked into propellers with you and what has resulted is usually a piece of work that has touched somebody. Sometimes it’s seen by millions of people and sometimes it’s seen by tens of people,” said Vachon. “But our movies came to life and made it to the screen because writers and directors trusted us with their stories and actors knew we were creating an environment that enabled them to give their best performance.”

Many of the honorees spoke about the mentors and industry giants who had helped them along the way. Close said she’d promised her World According to Garp director, George Roy Hill, that she’d thank him if she ever won an Oscar. “I never got the chance to thank the man who put me in my first movie. Now I can,” she said, holding her statuette up high. Scott, the director whose prolific career output includes Thelma & Louise, Gladiator, Black Hawk Down, Alien, Blade Runner, and The Martian, told a story in his video message about making his brother star in his very first project, the 1965 short film Boy and Bicycle. “I’m flattered and proud to accept this award, but I also accept it for Tony,” Scott said of his brother, who died in 2012. “His great work would certainly have earned this recognition.”

#3501. ‘DWTS’ Pro Jan Ravnik Throws Shade at Maks Chmerkovskiy During Livestream

Dancing With the Stars pro Jan Ravnik has fanned the flames of his ongoing feud with Maks Chmerkovskiy.

After Ravnik, 31, was told during a live backstage interview about his Tuesday, November 17, performances with partner Tatyana Ali, that his waltz was “beautiful,” he replied, “say that to Maks,” and pointed a directive finger towards the camera.

The professional dancer was joined by fellow pro Alan Bersten for the interview, with Bersten, 32, flashing a shocked face to the camera as he took in Ravnik’s cheeky remark.

The livestream moment was shared via a fan’s X account that night with the comments, “Ahhhhh not @JAnRavnik throwing shade at Maks !!!!!” and “Thank you to the person who caught this on TikTok.”

Ravnik’s comment comes after seemingly several barbs were recently sent back and forth between himself and Chmerkovskiy, 46, who have locked horns since October 2025 after Chmerkovskiy criticized Ravnik’s debut DWTS season.

Social media users reported online ahead of the Tuesday, November 10, episode of DWTS that Chmerkovskiy and fellow pro Gleb Savchenko had allegedly placed bets via a sports betting platform that Ali, 47, and Ravnik would be eliminated at the end of the night’s episode.

During an interview with USA Today after the episode wrapped, Ravnik said his anthem for this season of DWTS was Taylor Swift’s “The Smallest Man Who Ever Lived,” before raising his eyebrows for the camera.

The response sparked online fan speculation that he was referring to Chmerkovskiy.

In addition to comments made by Ravnik during Tuesday’s livestream, a post-episode interview with USA Today also seemingly referred to the betting drama. When asked for a message for fans, Ravnik said, “I hope you lose all your money,” which stopped Ali in her tracks.

“Well, OK, that was more of a general question but we got very specific,” she said as Ravnik fell back in a fit of giggles.

During the October 24, 2025 episode of Chmerkovskiy’s wife, Peta Murgatroyd’s “Penthouse With Peta” podcast, Chmerkovskiy said, “I’m sorry, Jan has absolutely no business being a pro on Dancing With the Stars,” adding that Ravnik had “zero foundation technique, quality [and] understanding of the partnership.”

Chmerkovskiy continued at the time, “How are you going to expect him to teach it and deliver that message in a format that is completely different from even ballroom dancing? We had this criticism weeks ago, and I’m like, ‘Bro, is anybody going to explain it to him?’”

Ravnik responded three days later with a TikTok captioned “Me When Anyone Talks Trash About Jan,” and, despite an apology from Chmerkovskiy over his initial comments, a subtle war of words has endured ever since.

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET.

#3500. Lil’ Kim Takes The Spotlight—With A Symphony

When you hear the name Lil’ Kim, a variety of images come to mind. She’s forever known as the force of nature from Brooklyn who turned the music industry on its head when she entered the scene, and her bodacious lyrics and unique fashion sense have kept her as a source of inspiration on your favorite designer’s mood board ever since. On November 18 and 19, to celebrate the music that cemented her icon status, Lil’ Kim will perform in front of a symphony orchestra at the Kings Theatre in Brooklyn, not far from her humble beginnings.

Today she’s less interested in being in the spotlight and more focused on raising her 12-year-old daughter, Royal Reign. In between practices for her performances, Lil’ Kim spoke with Vanity Fair to reflect on her career, how she spends her days, and her standout looks.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: What do you remember about putting your debut album, Hard Core, together?

Lil’ Kim: I remember Biggie and Un [Lance Rivera], who was the label owner that we had. I watched Un build a record label called Undeas, which [stood] for “Un ideas,” and then he finally sold it to Atlantic Records. At the time, we didn’t know the process, but we became Undeas-Atlantic. I remember Biggie having the idea of how he wanted my album to be red, and he explained it to me and Un. I was able to write according to how his idea was to present me, because when they met me, I was who I was—in high heels, jeans, motorcycle jackets, and furs at 13.

Portrait of members of R&B group 112 and rappers Notorious BIG and Lil’ Kim circa 1996

That’s incredible. It sounds like your fashion-icon status started very early. Was there anyone that you looked to back then? What inspired you to dress that way?

My mom was a big inspiration to me when it came to fashion, and so I looked to her for a lot of things. I used to wear her mink coat. She used to wear big sunglasses with her fur coats, with the diamonds and jewelry. She was always taking vacations and I would see her pack her stuff, and she would always have the cutest outfits. They were all matchy-matchy. It’s funny because she would have her outfit to go play tennis in and her outfit would match her tennis racket. So when I bought my big house, I bought a Chanel tennis outfit and I bought the racket to match it, because of my mom.

I love that. Do you keep up with tennis or specifically the ladies in tennis?

No, I haven’t in a while, but, of course, you know, Serena and Venus were like my heroes.

Well, maybe we need to see you on the court one day.

I know. I’m pretty sure I’m rusty, but I like to get out there, though. I used to beat my cousin’s butt back then.

How did the symphony performances come about?

My agents called me and they’re like, “Kim, what do you think?” And I was like, “That’s a freaking awesome idea.” I love performing with bands. And so I imagine that it could be very similar, if not very close. And I thought this could be something really different for me. Sometimes I even listen to classical music. I don’t have to know who the artist is, but I just put on a station and let it flow.

Do you have a favorite song from Hard Core?

I love “Queen Bitch”; it’s my favorite song. It’s still my favorite to perform. And “Crush on You.”

Salma Hayek, Donatella Versace, Pamela Anderson, and Lil’ Kim at Versace’s spring/summer 2001 fashion show

When it comes to fashion, you’re obviously on everyone’s mood board, from stylists to designers, so how important was fashion for you as part of the Lil’ Kim persona?

I just was being myself, honestly. When I first met Biggie, I was coming from my after-school job at Bloomingdale’s. I was probably 13 or 14 at the time, and they would let the teenagers work there.

But I had on a motorcycle jacket and high heels. And one of my best friends told Biggie, “You know, my girl can rap,” because we knew he was rapping around the way. And he was like, “I heard you can rap.” And I just laughed. He was like, “Yeah, see, I knew you didn’t know how to rap.” He was very condescending. He knew how to get you to do what you wanted to do, because I was really shy.

And then I started rapping, and he was blown away because I had on high heels. No one had ever seen someone just bust a rap in high heels. When Biggie, Un, and Jacob York started really talking to me, they didn’t want to change me because that was just what they were so blown away about. That was just who I was.

Do you think people ever misunderstood the way you presented yourself?

To be honest, I never really felt misunderstood by my hardcore fans—the kids my age and the younger kids, they totally got it. I think that’s why I had such a cult following and there was such pandemonium about me when I came out. They understood me. I think it was the older people and the politicians, those are the people who I think misunderstood me.

What did you think of the midterm elections and all of the women who broke barriers in the Senate and gubernatorial offices?

I’m going to be honest with you, I stay away from politics.

Are you keeping up with all of the changes within fashion today? When I listen to your music, you’ve mentioned so many designers and houses, and since then the creative directors have changed. Are you following all of the changes within fashion and seeing how you’re still a part of the conversation?

That’s what I’m trying to say. As a fashion icon, if you really her, and I’m considering myself really her, that’s never gonna change. That’s never going to change. I might put on a fur coat that my stylist or myself will get asked about, because I style myself a lot. And I was styling myself then.

Lil’ Kim and daughter, Royal Reign, on June 16, 2016, in New York City

Extremely rewarding. My daughter’s with me all the time. This world is so cruel and so evil; it’s so different. She’s my safe haven. I feel the extra need to keep her safe.

What does a regular day look like for you?

Lately, I’ve just been really getting into myself. I get up and go have a little spa day. I might take my daughter to go do whatever she wants.

Singer Mary J. Blige with Diana Ross and Lil’ Kim at the 1999 MTV Video Music Awards on September 9, 1999

How do you feel that we’re still talking about your MTV VMAs look in 1999?

I think it’s iconic and I love it. I love when they bring that up, because it was a fun day and it was so good to see people’s faces when they saw my outfit.

Are there any other looks that don’t get as much love as you wish that they did?

I don’t know, because most of the looks that I love, they get the love. There’s a look when I was on the cover of Nylon magazine and I had the teddy bear dress on; that’s one of my favorite looks. The Louis Vuitton look is one of my favorite looks; I love that look. A lot of the Chanel looks and the Versace and the Chanel in the hair.

Yellowjackets is arguably one of the best Paramount+ shows, although it required fans to get a Paramount+ subscription including Showtime. I'm personally a hardcore fan who is hyped about the fourth and final season's premiere this month. Folks are hoping to have Yellowjackets' biggest mysteries solved before it ends its run, and hopefully joins the ranks of TV shows that actually ended well. We know that the series guards it secrets from the public, but it turns out that even the cast is left in the dark about spoilers.

Yellowjackets' cast is an incredible multi-generational ensemble who tell the story across two timelines. The pressure is on for the Emmy-nominated series to stick the landing, and provide answers about various long-standing mysteries. In a recent interview with ScreenRant, Teen Shauna actress Sophie Nélisse was asked if she knew her character's fate ahead of time, to which she said:

No, we actually don't get the scripts more than like a week in advance, which is kind of fun because on set we're all sort of plotting and trying to reflect on what we have. We were coming up with our own theories of what the finale was going to look like, but we had no idea how they were going to get rescued, how their time in the wilderness would end. I obviously knew that Shauna was going to get married because we saw that.

Well, my mind is blown. While Yellowjackets fans are being kept away from spoilers, I had no idea how tight the security was for even the cast. They only got each new script a week in advance, so Nélisse and her costars weren't able to use the full arc of their character to inform each performance. Instead they had to take things episode by episode and play each moment with honesty without looking ahead.

Fans have lingering questions about the No Eyed Man as well as the mystery involving Crystal's dead body. While we're still in the dark for now, so was the cast. The Heated Rivalry actress went on to say:

We just kind of went day by day with it. We were just always so excited when we got a new script because, as the audience feels when they finish an episode, it always kind of leaves us on a cliffhanger. That's how, whenever we read a script, we'd all message in the group chat, being like, ‘Oh, this one is so good! I love this bit, and I love that bit.’

Celebrities: sometimes they really are just like us. Despite being the actors bringing Yellowjackets to life, they were left with episode cliffhangers in the midst of shooting Season 4. I have to wonder if Sophie Nélisse and her co-stars even know all the twists that are coming with the show's final season on the air.

Yellowjackets Season 4 will premiere on November 20th as part of the 2026 TV schedule. The pressure is on for the drama series to stick the landing, but it looks like we'll get plenty of surprises in the final set of episodes.

#3498. 20 Years Ago Today: The Best James Bond Movie Ever Made Was Released In Theaters

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There are very few franchises in cinema history that can compete with James Bond in terms of sheer viability across multiple decades. From "Dr. No," which kicked off cinema's most enduring franchise, to Daniel Craig's swan song "No Time to Die," 007 has endured. But 20 years ago, Bond reached his full potential as an icon of the silver screen.

20 years ago today, director Martin Campbell's "Casino Royale" first hit theaters. At the time, Craig was an up-and-coming star who wasn't a popular choice to take over as author Ian Fleming's beloved British creation. He was taking over for Pierce Brosnan, who had an uneven four film run that ended with arguably the worst James Bond movie of all time, "Die Another Day." To put it lightly, the pressure was on, but Campbell and Craig delivered in a huge way. "Casino Royale" is an undeniable masterwork of blockbuster filmmaking.

In stark contrast to "Die Another Day," which came out just four years earlier, "Casino Royale" was gritty, grounded, and opened up Bond to a new generation, while also serving as a welcome surprise to those who'd loved 007 for years. Opinions vary as they always do, but two decades removed, this pitch perfect piece of franchise filmmaking stands head and shoulders above everything that's come before or since. At the very least, it sits firmly in the top three with some room for debate.

What wasn't up for debate? Bond, James Bond was back, baby. Be it someone's first "Bond" movie or their 20th, this worked like gangbusters. It's the kind of movie that can make someone a fan of a franchise for life.

Just to show my hand, I've been watching "James Bond" for over 30 years and "Skyfall" was the movie that made me a lifelong fan. That said, I can admit that "Casino Royale" is very arguably the "better" movie, even if I personally enjoy "Skyfall" more. Every single time I watch it, I marvel at how perfect it is.

It certainly doesn't hurt that Martin Campbell has a real eye for 007. "GoldenEye" was the most important box office hit in "James Bond" history, as it had to relaunch the franchise following a six-year gap. Campbell is the man who knew how to bring Bond into the '90s with a fresh take. Similarly, when it was time to bring Bond into the 21st century, Campbell was called upon to work his magic. What's fascinating, though, is that "GoldenEye" and "Casino Royale" couldn't be more different.

"GoldenEye" was something of a grab bag, mixing some of the best elements of the Sean Connery and Roger Moore eras into one. "Casino Royale," on the other hand, was a full-blown origin story, adapting Ian Fleming's very first "Bond" novel. It was also very modern, totally willing to embrace the future and move away from the past. But that doesn't mean it forgot what Bond can and should be.

Campbell managed to get the most out of Craig's performance, turning him into both a handsome, charming devil of a man, as well as a ruthless killer. It's fun. It's glamorous. It's hair-raising. It's sexy. It's not so serious that it loses the fun along the way. It's truly the platonic ideal of what a "James Bond" movie should be, and the culmination of more than four decades of filmmaking up to that point.

"Casino Royale" has something for every fan. There are people who grew up with movies like "Goldfinger" who will always love that as the quintessential "Bond" movie, but those classics don't resonate with some modern viewers. There are those who relish the camp and deeply British sensibilities of something like "The Spy Who Loved Me," but that may not work for a younger viewer who is trying to understand who this 007 fellow is.

This movie encapsulates the Bond-ness of it all in a way that everyone can enjoy. It certainly doesn't hurt that Mads Mikkelsen's Le Chiffre is one of the greatest James Bond villains ever. Or that the big climax at the center of the film is at a poker table, rather than some giant action sequence. Don't get me wrong, we get plenty of action, but the poker game is a subversion of expectations and embraces a big part of Bond's history.

Then there's Vesper Lynd. Vesper Lynd in "Casino Royale" was the most difficult Bond girl to cast, but Eva Green ate the role up and gave an emotional core to the movie. A meaningful love interest is something that so many of the Bond films are missing, as he tends to think of women as "disposable pleasures," to quote Lynd. The relationship here raises the stakes, and the chemistry between Green and Craig is off the charts.

2012's "Skyfall" became the biggest Bond movie ever, but there's no way that would have happened if "Casino Royale" didn't tee up the ball so beautifully. This is the movie that this franchise is going to have to measure up to from now until the end of time. This set a new high-water mark for one of cinema's most long-lasting icons.

You can grab "Casino Royale" on Blu-ray from Amazon.

#3497. Pregnant Emilie Kiser Bawls While Marking 1.5 Years Since Son Trigg's Death

Lifestyle influencer Emilie Kiser has shared her heartbreak as she prepares to mark one-and-a-half years since the death of her son, Trigg.

“Bawled the whole way home from my hair appointment, just missing my Triggy so so much,” Kiser, 27, wrote over a Tuesday, November 17, Instagram Story photo that showed her sitting in her car as tears streamed down her face. “I’m just so f***ing sad … tomorrow if a year and a half since we’ve lost Trigg and I just, literally, can’t even believe it.”

The social media personality, who announced in July that she is pregnant after the May 2025 death of Trigg, 3, following a fall into the family’s backyard pool, added that the reality of the milestone had hit her earlier in the week.

“It already has hit me, this entire week, but … it’s so painful, and just so s***ty,” she said.

A subsequent Instagram Story featured a photo of Kiser’s reddened face as she stared blankly ahead. “I genuinely hate making others uncomfortable, like, sometimes that’s how I feel crying in front of people or it being noticeable that I’ve been crying,” she wrote over the top of it. “So now avoiding going into my home because I have contractors here.”

An earlier Instagram Story had explained that despite the sunny disposition she often exhibits via her social media posts, “social media is fake sometimes.” She added that she wasn’t immune from “masking how I really feel” and explained that it’s how she survives “most days so my brain doesn’t completely shut down.”

Kiser and her husband, Brady Kiser, lost their child at their Arizona home on May 12, 2025. Brady, 30, and Trigg’s brother Teddy, 19 months, were both home when Trigg was pulled unconscious from the pool.

Police officers arrived at the scene and began performing CPR before firefighters took over life-saving measures. Trigg was subsequently flown to Phoenix Children’s Hospital for further treatment and the Chandler, Arizona, Police Department confirmed to Us on May 18, 2025, that Trigg died.

On August 28 that year, Emilie broke her silence on the tragedy. “Loss of this magnitude feels impossible to put into words. I’ve spent days, weeks, months trying to find them and also take the time I’ve needed to digest the loss of my baby,” she wrote via social media at the time.
