#3485. Timothée Chalamet Talks ‘Dune 3,’ the Knicks, and His Hollywood Inspirations

Shoes on or off?” Timothée Chalamet asks, like any good New Yorker entering someone’s apartment. On is just fine.

He’s carrying a white paper deli bag—“starving,” he says—so I set him up at the dining table, where he unfurls a Lenwich Italiano. He devours it in less than two minutes. We’ve met before, but definitely never hung out at home. I think he’s friends with Frank Ocean, so I throw on Channel Orange. I had stocked up on a variety of beer and tea, can offer a coffee or a cocktail, but Chalamet wants New York City tap water, please, no ice.

Custom jacket by Haider Ackermann for Canada Goose; pants by Roa Hiking; backpack by Montbell.

I live in a one-bedroom in the East 60s, the second floor of an 1870 town house. The walls are white, the floors are black, and there are flowers from the bodega on the coffee table.

Chalamet is in earth-toned gorpcore, from the sand-colored Gnuhr puffer all the way down to a tawny pair of Roas, and would look equally at home camouflaged on the streets of Manhattan or trekking in the Dolomites, which he has recently done with his father. Both ears are pierced. Except for a navy blue novelty tourist cap which reads, in a comically fancy font, “Hvar, Croatia”—another recent vacation destination, with girlfriend Kylie Jenner—Chalamet’s color palette is pure Arrakis.

THE PROPHECY Timothée Chalamet, who will reprise his role as Paul Atreides – the chosen one – in Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, photographed in Iceland. Shirt by Prada.

He’s just come from the Fiorello H. LaGuardia High School of Music & Art and Performing Arts, his alma mater located directly across the park, where he spoke with a group of drama students. Tonight he’s going to a Yankees game with his mom, the former New York City Ballet prima ballerina, and his sister, Pauline.

Late lunch concluded, he relocates to the sofa. “Ahhh,” he says, taking a big seat and resting his right arm along the back.

He glances down at the old issues of Vanity Fair on my coffee table and comes to a stop on one in particular: June 1995. Courtney Love is on the cover, photographed by Herb Ritts, wearing massive white-feathered wings in homage to the Nike of Samothrace at the Louvre. Inside, there’s a Ritts portrait of a toddler Frances Bean.

OUTDOOR VOICE Timothée Chalamet and photographer Aidan Zamiri spent three days in Iceland for this shoot, code-named Caladan—the planet where Chalamet’s Dune character, Paul Atreides, was born.

“This wasn’t the crazy one,” I say, guessing at what he’s thinking.

Three years prior to this cover, in the September 1992 issue of Vanity Fair, Lynn Hirschberg profiled Love and quoted her saying that she used heroin before and at the beginning of her pregnancy. The story sparked a crisis for the young Cobain family that resulted in an investigation by the department of children and family services and Cobain threatening Hirschberg and her dog. In the annals of celebrity profiles, it goes down as one of the most scalding of all time.

Chalamet knows all about that story because he’s seen Montage of Heck, the Cobain documentary that features the Vanity Fair article. “It was mind-blowing to me because Lynn has only ever been to me just a figure of warmth...” Chalamet says, trailing off.

He puts the magazine back slowly, like it might burn him.

I’ll be honest with you: That’s not what’s about to happen here today. I’m not that scary, and he’s not using heroin. Nevertheless, this guy’s jumpy.

It’s dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days. Chalamet knows that better than anyone. At 30, he’s been famous his entire adult life. He’s dating one of the most visible women in the world. And he is acutely aware how a single comment in Vanity Fair could ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet. Earlier this year, during a no-holds-barred Oscar campaign for Marty Supreme, an offhand remark comparing the film industry to ballet and opera was met with outsize outrage, as some saw an opportunity to take Hollywood’s boy wonder down a peg. Those aware that he’s from a performing arts family knew what he meant. (“Is he wrong?” New York Times’ dance critic, Gia Kourlas, asked.) He doesn’t want to revisit that with me, perhaps because as he enters another awards season, he’s cautious in a way that only comes with experience.

In our 90 minutes together, Chalamet is both earnest and also reluctant to be profiled. He is by turns generous and guarded, confident and careful. He prefaces answers to no fewer than seven different questions by saying that he doesn’t want to sound “pretentious.” Truthfully, he never does. He’s protective of his personal life and will not discuss his girlfriend, nor much outside of filmmaking. “I wish I didn’t have to talk too much,” Chalamet says. And yet here he is, all across Iceland in our cover shoot, and now on my blue velvet sofa.

Like every conversation in late 2026, ours starts with AI. “Thou shall not make a machine in the likeness of a man’s mind,” Chalamet reminds me, is one of the opening lines of Dune, Frank Herbert’s seminal 1965 sci-fi novel. The story takes place in a world where computers are banned long after an AI apocalypse like the ones that are presaged by current-day tech CEOs and causing so much societal agita.

COLD MOUNTAIN Chalamet formed a community while making the first two Dune films. The third was “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” Boots by Timberland; scarf by Norlha; vintage pants by Arc’teryx Pro.

Chalamet tells me he’s reading The AGI Chronicles, tech journalist Kevin Roose’s new book that maps out the sprint to reach artificial general intelligence. He points out that the first four chapters of the book track the plot of Artificial, referring to Luca Guadagnino’s new Sam Altman biopic. “This is five seconds ago.” He recommended the book to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who later tells me Chalamet “found it to be not only informative, it’s helped with anxiety. The more you know, the less anxious you are about it.”

Just when everyone seems at least a little bit anxious about the end of the human species, along comes Dune’s computer-free vision of the future that is, as Chalamet puts it, “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.”

LIFE ON MARS “The whole thing is daunting,” says Chalamet about working on a franchise like Dune. Coat and shoes by Prada; pants by Stone Island.

You don’t need to have seen the conclusion of Denis Villeneuve’s trilogy to understand a few things about it. First of all, that it is enormous. Its scale is even bigger than The Odyssey’s. The grand vision of Villeneuve’s intergalactic war drama actually makes the adaptation of the West’s first epic poem (and presumed best picture front-runner so far) look like an exercise in restraint.

The production design of Dune: Part Three, set 20,000 years in the future, is largely inspired by the pangeographical past. There are aesthetic references as far-ranging as the samurai and SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism and the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua New Guinea, and perhaps more than any other single culture, ancient Egypt. And like the pyramids themselves, the visual effect of the film is mystical rather than technological, even though both obviously are technical achievements. (No AI was used in the making of Dune: Part Three.)

Chalamet gives Villeneuve all the credit for what he calls the “titanic” scope of the film, constructed on the foundation of the first two over the course of a decade. “It seems like he just kept building and becoming more ferociously in control of it,” he says. “Much like how Paul gets good at riding the sandworm, Denis took hold of these films.” The movie makes it easy to see how Star Wars—and particularly Anakin Skywalker’s character arc—is often considered derivative of Dune. (For the real heads: The story of Dune: Part Three is roughly equivalent to Star Wars episodes IV through VI, all in one film.)

“It’s huge, huge geography,” Chalamet says. “Do you think you could have done this when you were in your 30s?” Chalamet asked Villeneuve on set. “He goes, ‘No way.’ ” The director went on to tell him that he passed on a “huge sci-fi project” earlier in life that he wouldn’t even reveal to Chalamet, but Villeneuve “turned it down precisely because he felt like he didn’t have the tools yet.”

Production designer Patrice Vermette’s life-size sets were so imposing that Chalamet spent time on location in Budapest ahead of the film’s shoot, immersing himself in the palace of Arrakis so that he wouldn’t be distracted by its grandeur when the cameras rolled. “The whole thing is daunting,” Chalamet says. “I didn’t want any part of the day to be lost to ‘Wow, look at what I’m stepping into,’ ” he adds later. Compared to shooting the first two Dune films, he was more or less alone on set. Chalamet remembers it as “a more claustrophobic, isolated experience.” The way Villeneuve puts it: “Timothée created a bubble around himself which allowed him to delve more deeply into the depressive darkness of his character.” He was, after all, preparing to play a murderer.

FIELD OF VISION According to Chalamet, Dune, which is set 20,000 years in a computer-free future, feels “strangely superhuman, strangely very human.” Hoodie and eye cover by Adon; T-shirt by James Perse Los Angeles; necklace by Blackmerle.

Part Three encounters Chalamet’s antihero, Duke Paul Atreides (also known by his Fremen alias Usul, as the religious cult figure Muad’Dib, and the Padishah Emperor of the known universe—you got all that?), at the height of his totalitarianism and the nadir of his soul. Sixty-one billion is the number of deaths attributable to Atreides, who in the Herbert novels compares himself to Adolf Hitler and Genghis Khan. He is a “psychopath,” according to Florence Pugh’s Princess Irulan. Villeneuve tells me there was another detached paranoid figure he compared Atreides to: Howard Hughes.

To get into character, Chalamet studied the personalities of world leaders—“everyone good and bad” and particularly “megalomaniacs across human history.” He notes that “Frank Herbert wrote Messiah to course correct...the first Dune, where Paul is sort of revered as a hero.” He continues: “This is a cautionary tale against cults of personality and figures of charisma.” When I ask if Donald Trump was on his mind, he says “not particularly,” noting that power and its corrosive effects on the soul are “eternally prescient themes.” The film is ultimately a story of atonement—if not redemption—for a fallen messiah.

It was all this research that compelled Chalamet to shave off his globally recognized curly mop. “Decision fatigue is a real thing amongst the world leaders, good and bad, current and past.... The idea of not having to change clothes, not having to sweep the hair out of your face, simple shit like that.” And so Chalamet said goodbye to his Samson-like locks. Did he feel...“like Anne Hathaway in Les Mis?” Exactly. Or Natalie Portman in V for Vendetta, I offer. (He loves V for Vendetta.) Perhaps Demi Moore in G.I. Jane. “We would [shave] it basically every other day. My hair grows quickly, so we would get after it.” Today the curls, as you can see, have returned to their natural state. Power restored.

“Timothée has become much more ambitious as an actor,” Villeneuve tells me when I ask how he’s changed in the decade that they’ve worked together. “He is exploring new artistic paths in a highly exciting way.” Costar Javier Bardem says, “In a way, his growth has been almost chronological with that of his character. In Dune: Part Three, there is a real gravitas to him. He stands firmly in his place, with a confidence and authority that he has earned through his work, his sacrifices, his dedication, and his commitment as an actor and as a professional. You can see it and feel it, and it is incredibly reaffirming to witness.”

Safdie puts it like this: “I believe he’s like hi-fi sound. A good hi-fi system you can listen to in a tiny room and it makes the room feel huge. And he has that ability as an actor...his style of acting is larger-than-life realism.”

“He is always restlessly searching to keep the scene alive,” says Greta Gerwig, who directed Chalamet in Lady Bird and Little Women.“He needs room to scream a scene or whisper it or jump up onto a table or pirouette.”

MAN OF ACTION Chalamet wants his art to speak for itself: “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there.” Suit by Gucci; shirt by Harvey Bigg.

When I ask Chalamet if being famous his entire adult life prepared him to play a lonely-at-the-top emperor, he points to the moment in the first Dune when Paul and his mother, Lady Jessica, arrive on Arrakis and are greeted by the entire awe-inspiring army. “There were moments” in his own life, he says, when he realized about his relationship with the public: “Oh, something has shifted.”

Wandering around my apartment, Chalamet is observant and interested. “The picture in your bathroom looks like Greta.” He means Gerwig, though it’s actually Edie Sedgwick balancing on one leg in arabesque, cigarette in hand. (Sedgwick lived in this apartment during her Warhol years, and the picture was taken in the living room where we are sitting.) We look through the 1965 issue of Vogue, in which the picture originally ran.

He points out the French poster for The Graduate in the bedroom, in which a pink Matisse-like cutout of a woman’s elegant leg hovers in a thought bubble above Dustin Hoffman’s head. “I didn’t know it was called that,” he says. “Le Lauréat.” (One journalist recommended that I speak French with Chalamet, as they find him more open when they do. Sadly, I can hardly order dinner in French.)

He loves an Annie Leibovitz picture of Cindy Sherman made up as the sad clown in Edward Hopper’s 1914 Soir Bleu and points out monographs about Ed Ruscha and Harmony Korine on my bookshelf. (“Beast!” he declares about Korine.)

He sweetly asks me about a picture of me officiating my best friends’ wedding.

WORLD VIEWS “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central,” says Chalamet, a born and raised New Yorker.

We’re back on the sofa now. I’d asked Chalamet to do a little homework before our meeting: to come prepared to talk about his favorite movie performances. He was a diligent student, but instead came with four films and one play that specifically helped him get ready for his Vanity Fair cover shoot.

“Tree of Life,” he begins, citing Terrence Malick’s impressionistic masterpiece as the “biggest inspiration” for the cover shoot, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland. “It could have been accomplished over a half day in the studio,” Chalamet says, but they traveled thousands of miles because, as in Tree of Life, “the process is almost as important as the finished product.”

Next up is One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest. “It’s a kick-ass performance, and it’s provocative and heartwarming and full of life and one of the great movie performances of all time.” He cites Cloud Atlas, which the Wachowski sisters made years after The Matrix trilogy, as achieving the kind of scale that inspired the team to trek to the edge of Icelandic cliffs and inside waterfalls. (It’s also one of two films, along with Bruce Robinson’s 1987 Withnail and I, that Christopher Nolan has ever recommended to him.)

Chalamet whips out his orange iPhone—where he has incidentally started a new daily habit of playing chess—to show me the trailer for the Francis Ford Coppola–produced 1982 art house film Koyaanisqatsi, a hypnotic succession of increasingly uneasy urban vignettes, sped up and slowed down. “It’s about the humility you must feel as any person within the scale of the universe,” Chalamet says. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland, you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.” This one was recommended by Safdie and is clearly an inspiration for the relentless, kinetic pacing of his own movies as well. Chalamet is so close to Safdie that even the chess habit is inspired by the match that Safdie and Alfonso Cuarón continue in perpetuity.

“What’s interesting about Timmy is he’s incredibly curious and very sincere, but also has a pretty sharp sense of humor and can be quite jagged,” Safdie himself tells me a week later. “There’s a goofy seriousness to him. He likes to be provoked.”

SMOKE SHOW Next up for Chalamet? A top-secret collaboration with a “phenomenal” filmmaker. “It’s kind of a no-brainer.”

And finally, he gives me Man to Man, Tilda Swinton’s one-woman show currently on at London’s Royal Court Theatre. “It’s about the incredible futility of existence and a person losing their mind,” Chalamet says. “I liked it in this little program I created.”

I’ve never met any actor who prepared for a photo shoot the way he would for a role in a movie. I get the sense that’s just Chalamet’s way: Everything he does in public is considered part of the art. Everything except, perhaps, courtside appearances.

Little provokes Chalamet more than the New York Knicks, and it is the subject about which he gets most animated. “It’s the most quintessential New York team” for many reasons, he says, but chief among them is location, location, location. “It’s not like the Yankees or Mets, Giants, or Jets. It’s in the heart of Manhattan, and it reflected the agony of the New York experience for decades.” Chalamet says he lives two lives: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.”

When I ask what his greatest extravagance is, the immediate and definite answer is “sports tickets.” “Those away games weren’t cheap, but...it is the most fun I’ve had in my life as a human.” We know this. Because the best word to describe pictures of Chalamet courtside and in the Knicks locker room is simply ecstatic.

He tells me about traveling through the night from San Antonio back to New York after the Game 5 championship as an all-time life high. “I flew with people that had been working at the Garden for decades,” he says, explaining that Ben Stiller and Fat Joe were along for the ride on an MSG-owned plane. (“I don’t want to sound too out of touch,” he worries. I assure him the reader will understand that commercial airlines aren’t running 2 a.m. departures.) “It was just incredibly raucous, everyone celebrating.”

DISTRESSED OUT Or is he? Chalamet isn’t pressed about trying to emulate his heroes: “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic.”

Chalamet says he will always remember Jalen Brunson’s quiet leadership as the hallmark of the season overall. “It was not the cult of personality” you might expect to lead a championship team, he notes. “It was someone actually quite soft-spoken, reserved, and hardworking, and unassuming.”

On topics other than basketball, he is less enthusiastic. “My work is my bones and muscles. I have little interest in putting more of myself out there,” he says. What’s something that no one asks you that you wish they would? “Nothing. I mean, nothing. I’m not being passive-aggressive about this interview at all, but I think...” he trails off. Chalamet points at the speaker, which is still playing Frank Ocean. “He’s one of the rare people where the vacuum of what’s out there about him helps drive the...” “Curiosity?” I offer. “Beyond curiosity, how brilliant his artistry is. But the economy of movies,” Chalamet says, thinking. “You got to sell a lot of tickets.”

Which is exactly the reason that we’re sitting here together now. Who is his dream collaborator, living or dead? After a long silence, I tell him he can pass. “Okay. Pass.” What does he think of David Ellison’s Skydance taking over Warner Bros., the studio behind Dune? “I’m going to hit a Frank Ocean and be mysterious,” is all he says.

Leonardo DiCaprio once gave him very solid advice. Two rules: no superhero movies, no hard drugs. Would Chalamet have any advice for a 22-year-old getting started? “I think the best thing you can do is encourage people to be confident in what they believe is best for them.” Plus, he adds, “the Kane Parsons of it all brought me tremendous humility,” referencing the 21-year-old YouTuber turned director of the staggeringly successful Backrooms.

He’s vague about future projects. “I got one thing with a phenomenal filmmaker,” he says. “It’s kind of a no-brainer project, and should it get announced, I think you’ll see what I mean.”

Would he ever return to the character of Elio, the protagonist of Call Me by Your Name that gave him his star turn? “A great question. Never say never, but...I’ve grown up with the mindset that you don’t really go near something that is so near and dear to people.” So, that’s a no. “Now, to work with Luca again? In a heartbeat.”

GAME BOY As Chalamet sees it, there are two ways of living his life: one as himself and one as “fan with a capital F.” Jacket by Chrome Hearts; headlamp by Nitecore.

Is there any actor, or artist of any kind, after whose career he would like to model his own? “Who was [Bob] Dylan looking at? Dylan.” He broke the mold, I offer. “He created the mold.” Chalamet wants to be an original too (and perhaps this is what he meant when he declared that he was in “pursuit of greatness” at the 2025 SAG Awards). “It’s less sexy to some degree to wade out in the unknown, but it’s more authentic,” he says. “Especially in the movie industry where people could feel like, Oh, that was the golden age.... You gotta cook it up in a unique way.”

Around 6 p.m., Chalamet gets up off the couch and suits back up in his gorpcore. The Yankees game starts in just a couple of hours, and he has to shower and collect his mom and sister and make his way to the Bronx. I walk him downstairs, amble down the stoop, and almost want to say: Look! We survived!

The Last of Us cast will be saying goodbye to each other and the Clickers soon.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Last of Us is a TV show that has meant a lot to a lot of people, as it has successfully translated the emotional core of the hugely popular video game and built on the complexity of the character relationships. The final season, anticipated to debut in 2027, is sure to be emotional for fans, too. So it’s not at all surprising to hear that the cast is emotional as they get to the end of filming and will have to say goodbye to each other.

An HBO show that got the world talking from the moment it debuted, the post-apocalyptic drama started by following Joel (Pedro Pascal) as he escorted the teenage Ellie (Bella Ramsey) across a devastated United States ravaged by a fungal infection that had turned people into violent creatures. With Season 3 delving deeper into the journey of Joel’s brother, Tommy Miller, actor Gabriel Luna not only has to say goodbye to a character he’ll know much better, but he’ll also be leaving the cast and crew behind after bidding them an emotional farewell. Here’s what he told Entertainment Weekly about the emotions that are already starting to swirl:

Oh man, a lot of emotions are going around. But right now I think we’re all too tired to feel them. [Laughs.] Because it’s just massive. Obviously I can’t give anything away, but people who’ve played the game know the level of the scope of what we’re dealing with here towards the end of the story. I’m so proud of Bella [Ramsey], Kaitlyn [Dever], and Kyriana [Kratter], who’s joined the cast, for being the tip of the spear and shouldering the weight of this production and what it requires from them.

If you played The Last of Us games, you knew that Abby would be seen on the show as a villain after killing Pedro Pascal's Joel. No matter her motivation or the extent of her own trauma, it would be challenging for viewers to understand the actions of someone taking out such a beloved character. And then, the Season 2 finale ended with the focus shifting to Kaitlyn Dever's Abby, who will take center stage in The Last of Us Season 3.

In a world like the one portrayed in The Last of Us, where everything is heightened as you just try to survive and not get killed or infected, emotions understandably run high for the cast helping bring that world to life. And even though Tommy comes in and out of the story, The Terminal List actor can’t help but be impressed by how the Ellie, Abby, and Lev actors are handling everything required of them, as they head closer to the finish line. He went on to say:

The bulk of my work was back in the summer, and then I’d go back and forth and come in for two, three weeks of time, but they’re here every day and doing the lion’s share of the work.

Since the Naughty Dog video game-turned-TV series is a massive production, it sounds like there’s going to be a prolonged series of goodbyes taking place as storylines are wrapped up and actors depart. Gabriel Luna not only has to process the emotion of saying goodbye to his own character and wrapping up a story that he likely feels very connected to after three seasons, but he also has to handle the departure of each of his co-stars. That’s a lot of emotions for the Dexter: Resurrection star, who will probably be exhausted by the time it’s all said and done. He pretty much said just that:

We’re getting to the end of it, and people are starting to wrap, and we’re giving them their flowers, and then they’re heading off, and one by one, the family is dwindling down to just the final few. We’re about to get a welcomed break and respite from what we’ve been doing, and then we have to come back and finish strong after the holiday. We’re so excited for this thing to come out.

I can only imagine the tears that will be flowing and the emotions that will be felt as the final days of the HBO series come to an end, and everyone says their final goodbyes. Fans anxiously anticipating the third season will have to pack their patience pants while waiting for details on when it will officially premiere. In the meantime, the first two seasons of The Last of Us are streaming with an HBO Max subscription.

#3482. This '80s R-Rated Superhero Movie Is Unlike Anything Marvel Or DC Has Made

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

We've been living in a world of mass entertainment dominated by superheroes and comic book characters for more than 25 years now, dating back to Marvel's earlier blockbuster hits like "X-Men" and "Spider-Man." Even small screen stuff like "The Walking Dead" has comic book roots. But decades before any of that, an indie film pioneer made a superhero movie unlike any other.

Lloyd Kaufman is independent film, in many ways, as the founder of Troma Entertainment. His media empire was built on the backs of low-budget schlock like "Surf Nazis Must Die" and "Pterodactyl Woman from Beverly Hills," among many others. But Kaufman's defining hit came in 1984 in the form of "The Toxic Avenger," an ultra violent, campy, R-rated superhero affair. It remains a distinct piece of punk rock cinema more than 40 years removed, unmatched in its insanity by anything Marvel or DC has done on screen.

The movie takes place in the fictional town of Tromaville, known as the toxic waste capital of America. A bullied young janitor in a popular gym falls into a vat of toxic waste and turns into a super strong but disfigured man. He begins cleaning up the streets from evildoers in an often funny yet violent fashion.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a long history on screen and is now a cult legend, but that legend began in '84, at a time when superheroes were far from bankable fare in the mainstream. Co-directed by Michael Herz and Kaufman himself, the resulting movie can't be accused of being high art, but it's one heck of a wild swing, and a testament to what the indie filmmaking spirit can accomplish.

At the time, Hollywood had only had the occasional superhero movie hit it big. "Superman: The Movie" in 1978 being the biggest one, while Batman didn't become a box office hero until 1989. Even that movie just led to the "Batman" franchise taking off rather than a broader trend of superheroes becoming big business. The '90s saw many try but few succeed, with stuff like "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles" more the exception rather than the rule.

All of this to say, when Lloyd Kaufman decided to make a dark superhero comedy — an R-rated and super violent one no less — it wasn't exactly a recipe for success. At least not on paper. But decades before "Deadpool" broke the Marvel mold by going R-rated and injecting comedy into the genre, "The Toxic Avenger" dared to venture into that territory.

What's more, Kaufman and Co. did it on a shoestring budget of well under $1 million. "Deadpool" gets a lot of credit for being low-budget, but it still cost north of $50 million. What Kaufman pulled off with latex, old school special effects, and can-do indie spirit is nothing shy of impressive. Even those who are put off by the nature of this sort of exploitation film should be impressed by what was accomplished here with so little.

"The Toxic Avenger" has a demented sense of humor, and it doesn't give us a typical hero either. Toxie isn't a square-jawed, muscle-bound vigilante. He's a mutant who decides to clean up the streets with straight-up violence. The film has more in common with revenge driven horror/thrillers than it does any mainstream superhero movie. All the same, it became a cult hit and started a wildly unlikely franchise.

"No theater would play it," Lloyd Kaufman said of "The Toxic Avenger" to Parallax View in 2010. "We couldn't get one theater to play it anywhere and then we took it to Cannes and not one deal. Nothing! And then a few months later we got one movie theater in Greenwich Village, New York, and there was a line around the theater."

That single theater paved the way for more to follow. This was also at the dawn of the VHS home video craze, which is where the movie really thrived — so much so that Kaufman eventually produced a series of sequels. That includes 1989's "The Toxic Avenger Part II" and "The Toxic Avenger Part III: The Last Temptation of Toxie," also released in '89. Much later, "Citizen Toxie: The Toxic Avenger IV" would arrive in 2000. A gore-soaked remake of "The Toxic Avenger" starring Peter Dinklage was also released in 2025.

Kaufman's crown jewel is an elbow grease style, gory, raunchy, rubber-suit take on superheroes that doesn't resemble anything we've seen in the 2000s, really. Sure, "Clayface" brought body horror to the DC Universe, but it's completely without a sense of humor. It's also slick and relatively expensive (for a horror movie).

It was cutting edge then and it's impressively distinctive even now. More than that, "The Toxic Avenger" helped make the empire that is Troma. It's easy to write it all off as schlock, but Troma has been a haven for indie film for decades, with filmmakers like James Gunn ("Guardians of the Galaxy") cutting their teeth there. Without this movie, who knows if the empire as we know it even exists?

You can grab "The Toxic Avenger" on 4K, Blu-ray, or DVD from Amazon.

#3481. High-Protein Packaged Foods May Not Be As Healthy As They Look

Of the three major macronutrients—protein, carbs, and fat—protein has the best reputation, and it’s fairly well deserved. We need significant amounts of protein in our diet, and nothing particularly bad happens if we get too much. Dietary protein helps you build muscle, and if you’re trying to lose weight it helps stop you from losing too much muscle along with the fat. It also helps to make meals feel filling. Great! But.

Once the general public gets the idea that something is good for you, the companies that make packaged food start putting it in everything. Or, they make products where the good-for-you thing features prominently on the label, whether or not there is very much inside. So a lot of packaged food now boasts protein on the label. Here’s what you should ask yourself about those foods:

Take a close look here—sometimes a food will boast of a certain amount of protein per package but the package contains two or three servings. Other times, the protein per serving is correct, and we're supposed to be excited to have, say, 7 grams per serving. That's just not very much—and certainly not worth paying extra or choosing a less-delicious food just for those few added grams.

It’s good to know how much protein you need in your diet. If you’re not gaining or losing weight, and not doing very much exercise, a 150-pound person only needs about 54 grams of protein a day. (I've done the math for various body weights here.) If you’re working out a lot, or if you’re trying to gain or lose weight (yep, either way), that same 150-pound person will need more like 81 to 95 grams of protein per day. More is OK, but not necessary.

So if you’re trying to get 90 grams per day, 30 grams per meal is a reasonable amount to shoot for. Coincidentally, 30 grams is the amount of protein that tends to make a meal feel satisfying. You can do the math to figure out whether a protein-added product is going to be helpful in your day’s diet.

I think this is the most important question about protein-added foods. It’s not hard to get protein in a meal; meats, dairy, tofu, beans, and grains all tend to supply plenty. So what is this protein-added thing you’re considering, and are you eating it instead of a traditional meal?

Here’s an example. If I’m heading straight from the gym to run some errands, and I need something to substitute for a meal—yeah, this isn’t great planning, but sometimes it happens—a protein bar with 20 grams of protein is a step in the right direction. Much better than a candy bar, anyway.

But then there are things like this "protein mix" trail mix: 7 grams of protein with 200 calories. A double serving would be 400 calories and only 14 grams of protein. Hardly a great choice if your goal is just to add to your protein intake for the day.

And then there are the chips that my kid, for a time, couldn't stop eating. He loves Doritos and such; on a whim, we bought him some protein chips (yes, these are a real thing). Are they better for him than the equivalent amount of Doritos? Arguably, sort of yes. But then he started arguing that since they have protein, he should be able to eat them in place of dinner. We nixed that, but admit it: Are you having that same argument with yourself, feeling better about a snack food because it contains extra protein? If so, the marketing is working—you’re feeling good about your supposedly healthy choices, even though you’re just eating a bag of chips.

#3480. Timothée Chalamet Came Over for Lunch—and a Cover Story

The history of actors appearing in Vanity Fair goes back about as far as the movies themselves. Making a studio-orchestrated, Edward Steichen–captured debut in the pages of this magazine was a milestone in the careers of Gary Cooper, Gloria Swanson, Anna May Wong, and dozens of others, many of whom never made it to Technicolor.

On more than one occasion, the idea of Timothée Chalamet as the last male movie star has been a debate here at the office, usually ending in uneasy agreement: He is one of very few left, maybe the only one of his generation. He is in the tradition of Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio in that his knowability runs inverse to his fame. Like other endangered species, his extreme rarity makes him celebrated and isolated in equal measure. And with each of these stars, one rule usually holds true: The bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.

All of which is why we are thrilled to have Chalamet on our cover as he sets out to open the final, breathtaking installment of Denis Villeneuve’s Dune trilogy. He and our team, led by photographer Aidan Zamiri, fashion editor Taylor McNeill (with whom I was an assistant at this magazine in 2010), and VF global creative director Jennifer Pastore, trekked to Iceland for a multiday shoot to capture his cover story “A Star on Planet Earth.” Everyone involved—including and especially Timothée—approached it more like a film, or maybe a music video, than a typical cover, and there is a spiritual quality that runs throughout the pictures. “I love that being on the edge of a cliff in Iceland,” Timothée tells me, “you get the same feeling as being in Grand Central.”

Timothée also had the idea that I write the cover story myself, and while I was reluctant, I eventually thought, Why not mix it up? He came over to my apartment in early October for a conversation about Dune; his career; the careers of other actors, musicians, and painters; and especially the careers of the New York Knicks. I took away from our meeting that he may be a movie star, sure, but he approaches everything as an artist. The writing process is a humbling one, though—okay, it’s agony—and since filing the cover story, I have come to believe that every editor really should write a feature now and again to make us more understanding of our writers. Perhaps once a year. Consider it a new rule at Vanity Fair.

Timothée and I were both reading Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles when we met up, and he pointed out that the first several chapters of the book might as well have been the source material for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s new film starring Andrew Garfield and Yura Borisov. The film presents a villain origin story of OpenAI’s cofounders, particularly CEO Sam Altman. It is the natural inheritor to David Fincher and Aaron ­Sorkin’s 2010 film, The Social Network, which similarly helped answer the how-did-we-get-here question for another quite recent era of technology.

In case you missed it, Altman was recently on the cover of Vanity Fair, sitting atop our revived New Establishment list. It inspired a torrent of furious reader feedback, including a few death threats. I understand that those messages were rooted in genuine fear of this technology and ire toward its Dr. Frankenstein founders (and me, by extension, for covering them). But reporting on the powerful—whether power is granted by elections or equities or zettaflops of compute—has always been the mandate of this magazine and will continue to be. We’ll keep the movie stars too.

#3479. How To Watch The Social Reckoning At Home

"The Social Reckoning" is finally hitting the home market. It will become available to buy or rent on digital starting November 24, 2026, prior to its physical media release on January 12, 2027.

In case you're unfamiliar with "The Social Reckoning" writ large, here's the gist. Almost two decades after he won an Academy Award for writing the screenplay for "The Social Network," a 2010 dramatization of the founding of Facebook directed by David Fincher, Aaron Sorkin decided to make a sequel that focuses on what Facebook has become in the 2020s. Jesse Eisenberg, who earned an Oscar nod for playing Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Network," declined to return to the role and was replaced by "Succession" veteran, Emmy and Tony winner, and Sorkin's "The Trial of the Chicago 7" collaborator Jeremy Strong. With Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Betty Gilpin, and Billy Magnussen starring alongside Strong, the project seemed almost too big to fail before it premiered in theaters on October 9, 2026.

Fail it did, though. Though it reportedly only lost a couple million for Sony (per Deadline), the film absolutely underperformed at the box office, and its rating on Rotten Tomatoes is a middling-to-bleak 54%. So what happened here? Well, from my perspective, "The Social Reckoning" is just a bad movie ... and /Film's chief film critic Chris Evangelista agrees with me. What went wrong as Sorkin tried to make a legacy sequel to one of the best films of the 21st century? Quite a lot actually!

I'll circle back to the "Social Network" of it all shortly, but the bottom line here is that "The Social Reckoning" just ... stinks to high heaven. From the embarrassing prologue featuring Portia Doubleday as a caricature named Kayleigh (I'm not kidding) to the fact that Aaron Sorkin keeps forcing Oscar winner Mikey Madison into outfits that would make her title character from "Anora" blush (in the name of corporate espionage), I found "The Social Network" to be a uniformly dreadful watch from start to finish. Not only is the script clunky as all hell — unfortunately, an ongoing problem with many of Sorkin's recent screenplays — but the story is attempting to make some sort of larger point that doesn't just fall flat but thuds directly to the floor. We already know social media makes everyone angry and insane, and we also know that social media has contributed to right-wing radicalization. Sorkin making a movie that beats us over the head with these two ideas and also ends in a full recreation of the January 6, 2021 insurrection is just as bad as it sounds in theory.

It's also incredible to me that Sorkin managed to cast a lot of great actors and coach them into giving some of the worst performances of their careers. Madison is an enigmatic and compelling performer, and Sorkin transforms her into the robotic Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen, a deeply unlikable person who doesn't seem to understand human behavior. Jeremy Allen White's journalist Jeff Horwitz is nothing but an exposition machine, and Jeremy Strong's Mark Zuckerberg has no interiority and sounds like Kermit the Frog. The only person who's good in this movie is Bill Burr. Think about that for a second.

"The Social Network" might be one of my very favorite movies of all time, but I can tell you, from a completely unbiased perspective, that "The Social Reckoning" is a wholly undeserving sequel to that 2010 masterpiece. It's clear now, with plenty of hindsight and movies like this, that "The Social Network" was good because of director David Fincher and despite Sorkin. To be fair to Sorkin, he basically admitted that to The Hollywood Reporter after "The Social Reckoning" got soundly panned.

"I would have rather David Fincher directed it — I would rather David Fincher direct everything — but David has an exclusive deal at Netflix, and this was owned by Sony," Sorkin told the outlet on their "Awards Chatter" podcast. Not only did Sorkin also admit that he's "very worried that the parts of directing that [he's] not good at are those parts that you can't learn," he also said, "I was surprised by how little of the science of filmmaking I'd managed to absorb [from other directors] ... I have no visual sensibility, it turns out."

I have to agree with him. Despite the same cinematographer — Jeff Cronenweth — working on both "Network" and "Reckoning," the sequel is visually bland, unimaginatively shot, and even recycles a couple reaction and establishing shots throughout its run time. Basically, "The Social Reckoning" is a poorly made film that I cannot in good conscience recommend; in fact, I'd recommend you just watch "The Social Network" instead. But if you're still interested, you can check out "The Social Reckoning" at home once it's available.

#3478. Everything You Should Know About Black Friday 2026 Sales: Early Deals, Dates, and Retailers

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always vet all of our deals for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

Follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Prime Day and Black Friday are the two best times of the year to get the best deals on most purchases. Of course, depending on what you're shopping for, you might find other opportunities throughout the year, but in general, Prime Day and Black Friday have the best sales.

#3476. Cillian Murphy's 28 Years Later: Part III Will Only Happen Under One Condition, Says Director Danny Boyle

Are we going to see "28 Years Later: Part III?" Director Danny Boyle is certainly interested in doing it and Alex Garland has written a script. The problem? Money. This year's "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" finally delivered the moment fans have been waiting for, bringing back Cillian Murphy as Jim. It was a small appearance teeing up something much larger in a presumed third installment. As Boyle recently explained, that movie is only going to happen if they can find the money.

Speaking recently with Deadline during an event for his new movie "Ink," Boyle's tabloid media origin story that will make you feel sick, the Oscar-winning director addressed the status of the third and presumably final entry in the "28" franchise. "There is a plan for a third part of '28 Years Later.' Alex has written a fantastic script," Boyle said. "We gotta raise the money to make it."

Sony Pictures produced both "28 Years Later" and "The Bone Temple." And while "28 Years Later" killed it at the box office, the sequel didn't. That's why Sony isn't eager to give it the green light. Speaking further, Boyle said that the third installment would bring the whole franchise to a close:

"[Cillian Murphy]'s up for it, and it's a fantastic part. Alex has written this fantastic part for him. Those of you who saw 'The Bone Temple,' the second part to '28 Years Later,' he's teased at the end of that. The third film does complete the story in a beautiful, mathematically perfect way, in which the circle is closed."

Creatively speaking, critics and audiences generally agreed that both of the recent "28" movies were damn good. But Hollywood is a business and money became an issue pretty quickly. "28 Years Later" made $151 million against a budget in the $60 million range. That was good enough. "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" flopped at the box office though, bringing in just $58.5 million worldwide on a similar budget. Unfortunately, the math doesn't math for anyone who wants to make money in this business.

That's why "28 Years Later: Part III" probably won't happen. Admittedly, "probably" is doing some heavy lifting there. Cillian Murphy is an Oscar-winning actor for his work in "Oppenheimer," Danny Boyle is an Oscar-winning director, and Alex Garland is an Oscar-nominated screenwriter. It's a powerhouse team. That makes it unlikely but not impossible.

The most realistic path to getting it made would be partnering with a streaming service. Netflix is releasing Boyle's new movie "Ink" and the streamer also has a partnership with Sony. That would be the logical choice. But if Boyle and Garland want it as a more traditional theatrical release? That's where it gets more complicated and far less likely.

As for where it all went wrong? The bonkers ending in "28 Years Later" left audiences divided, for one. There was also a very short, roughly six-month gap between installments, which seemingly hurt more than it helped. But playing Monday morning quarterback doesn't help now. It's really about Boyle and co. getting creative to see if they can cobble together the money to bring this story to a close.

#3475. Why Websites Show the Wrong Server Location When You Use a VPN

There are many reasons why someone might use a VPN, but most often, it’s to conceal your real geographic location or prevent websites from tracking your online activity. It can also be a way to get around location-based restrictions that stop you from accessing certain websites or platforms.

When you connect to a VPN server in the United States, websites are supposed to detect that your online traffic is originating from the U.S. That way, you can access online platforms that use IP filters to block non-U.S. traffic or circumvent regional censorship when travelling outside the U.S. But if you connect to a VPN server in the United States while you’re vacationing in Mexico, and a website thinks your IP address is from Brazil, that might not solve your problem and may even add unnecessary complications.

If you’ve encountered something similar with your VPN provider, there are several fixes you can try. Depending on why your IP location is being misinterpreted, one of these should help you access the internet from the server location of your choice.

IP geolocation isn’t infallible. Websites rely on third-party IP databases to look up your location based on your current IP address. Maxmind, which has one of the largest such databases in existence, claims that its GeoIP products have a 99.8% accuracy. Lesser-known providers with smaller IP databases may be far less accurate.

Websites can also use more than just your IP address to estimate your location. For example, they can send WebRTC requests to your browser or directly query your device’s GPS. Moreover, VPN providers often have physical servers in one country while their IP addresses are registered to another country, and this discrepancy can also create issues. Let’s take a closer look at each of these problems individually, so you can find the fix that works best for you.

WebRTC is an open-source technology that lets your browser reduce latency when engaged in high-bandwidth tasks like streaming or video calls. Based on the IETF standard RFC 8828, it lets a website choose between your VPN server and your real IP address so it can establish the quickest path to transmit large amounts of data and reduce wait times or buffering.

But the catch with WebRTC is that it exposes both your VPN server and ISP-assigned addresses to websites, which can reveal your real IP location and cause websites to reject your VPN server country. Firefox now comes with built-in protections to prevent WebRTC leaks, while Chrome and Edge support third-party extensions like WebRTC Control that you can use to eliminate these issues. To check if your browser is leaking your real IP address during WebRTC requests, you can use a free tool like BrowserLeaks.

Even when a browser isn’t leaking your real IP address, DNS resolvers may fetch inaccurate location information if their nearest servers are too far from your current location. For example, a user in São Paulo may be geolocated to Chile when using Google Public DNS because that’s where Google’s nearest resolvers are located.

If you toggle on DNS leak protection in your VPN app, this will force websites to use your VPN’s resolver to perform DNS lookups. That often solves the problem, but, again, you can confirm the fix worked through a service like BrowserLeaks or IPLeaks.

Websites rely on IP databases like Maxmind, IP2Location, IPinfo, etc. to look up your exact location, but these databases get outdated quickly and need constant updating. Most of these databases also correct errors on request, but that takes some time. Also, each website has its own rules for how often it queries IP databases for updates.

Even when locations are updated in the actual database, a website may be sitting with outdated information unless it actively has refreshed it recently. MaxMind recommends doing this at least twice a week, but that’s ultimately up to the specific website.

VPN providers often rely on virtual servers that use IP addresses registered in a different region than the server’s physical location. For example, ExpressVPN notes that it serves IP addresses in Bolivia, Ecuador, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela through servers located physically in Brazil.

While this is usually to help with the lack of local infrastructure or strict surveillance laws in the region, many databases and analytics tools will flag the discrepancy for websites, leading to confusion and inconsistency regarding your actual server location. In these cases, your best bet is to switch your VPN server or use a dedicated IP address by signing up for a paid add-on for your VPN.

Before investing in a specific solution, it’s better to do a thorough lookup to make sure why your IP address is pointing to the wrong location and whether a WebRTC or DNS issue, virtual servers, or something else is the cause. Here’s how I’d go about it, step by step:

We’ll start by recording your baseline IP address, country, city, and ASN. With your VPN disconnected, navigate to IPConfig.co on your browser to grab your default IP details. I like this tool because it’s free and uses echoip to pull your location data straight from Maxmind. If you prefer using Terminal instead of your browser, you can also run curl ifconfig.co/json to grab these details in plain text format.

Now connect your VPN server. Then visit IPConfig.co again to note down the changed details.

Make sure the Country and Timezone fields match your current VPN server location. Also make sure the ASN (organization) field does not list your home ISP.

In case these details do not match your VPN server, run a WebRTC leak test and a DNS leak test using BrowserLeaks. If either of these tests doesn’t return your VPN server’s IP address, you’ve found your culprit.

If both the leak tests come back clean but a specific site still gets your location wrong, the issue is likely originating from an outdated database or virtual server.

There’s no surefire way to solve IP location mismatches for good. But if it happens often enough to disrupt your internet use, you can consider switching to a different VPN server and getting a browser add-on that prevents WebRTC leaks. If that doesn’t work, I’d consider buying a dedicated IP address that isn’t based on a virtual server. While many IP databases like MaxMind or IP2Location also have ways to request a location correction, that takes a while to go through and isn’t worth the effort unless it’s a permanent IP address registered through your ISP.

Prince Harry, Meghan Markle and their two kids, Archie and Lilibet, have been adapting to a completely new life in the U.K. these past few months. However, some recent reports claim the family may already be getting ready to head back to Southern California to spend Christmas this year. That leads to the question: Why aren’t they allegedly starting new traditions across the pond?

The Royal Family famously spends their Christmas holiday at the Sandringham Estate in Norfolk. However, while Prince Harry may have grown up doing Christmas at the countryside property, he and Meghan only spent two holidays there – a month after they got engaged in 2017 and their first Christmas as a married couple in 2018. New claims by InStyle speculate that since they broke the tradition eight years ago, they aren't expecting this year to be any different despite the geographical convenience.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle spent their first two Christmas holidays with the Royal Family at Sandringham Estate. When that time of year rolled around in 2019, they had already formally separated from the Royal Family and appeared in a candid documentary interview where Harry said he and Prince Williams were "on different paths." So in 2019, they decided to spend the holidays privately in Canada with a nine-month-old Archie. And, in March 2020, they stepped away from being senior royals.

It’s expected that Harry and Meghan will share a more intimate holiday season with Meghan’s mother, Doria Ragland, as they usually do. While it’s been suggested they’d likely end the year in the U.S. (via People), a source with the Daily Mail reports Doria may be the one to head to the U.K. instead. Nothing’s been confirmed, but another reason why they aren’t going to the Sandringham Estate could be because they are simply not invited, per an October report:

They know it would be too awkward and too difficult [to spend Christmas with the royal family]. They also know they’re not going to be invited, and they’re not waiting for an invitation.

It's also worth taking into account that Meghan Markle and her mother have been reportedly leaning on each other following Markle’s father facing allegations of possessing child sexual abuse material. Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested by federal agents on November 6 and could serve prison time.

Over in the U.K., the couple reportedly haven’t found their forever home yet since relocating in August. They are currently living at a friend’s private estate in the Cotswolds. Perhaps they are searching for familiarity this holiday season after the big move?

In a 2025 email sent to followers of her lifestyle brand, As Ever, Markle said she was planning on spending the holiday that year with “pajamas all day, some Scrabble or Sequence (or Candyland for the kids), music playing, candles flickering, dogs snoring, endless grazing; the laughter, the sidebars, the deep breaths (you know the ones), the fun, and the memories.” The Royal Family’s Christmas traditions, on the other hand, involve a black-tie dinner and attending service at St Mary Magdalene Church on Christmas morning.

Markle has shared her love of Christmas before, calling it her favorite holiday and even making a special called With Love, Meghan: Holiday Celebration, which you can stream now with a Netflix subscription. Juggling the holidays is rarely easy, even for a power couple like those two.

#3473. Who Killed Fashion Founders Bryan Walker and Michelle Min?

Panoramic Hill looms above the UC Berkeley campus, a tree-covered neighborhood cut by steep paths and outdoor staircases. Century-old homes by brand-name architects like Bernard Maybeck and Walter Steilberg dot the incline, which straddles the border of Berkeley and Oakland. Each residence is worth millions; increase the amount for the occasional bit of newer construction. Unlike the busy urban streets below, the area is incredibly quiet. That’s one of the reasons everyone heard the shots.

“I have that stored in my memory, as I will for the rest of my life,” Daniella Salzman tells me, looking out her window at the former home of Michelle Min and her husband, Bryan Walker. The couple, creators of the Bryn Walker clothing brand, were found just outside their residence around 10:45 a.m. on October 2, 2026, shortly after neighbors called 911 to report the sound of gunfire. Initial confusion about jurisdiction sent police from both Berkeley’s and Oakland’s departments to the scene.

By the time paramedics arrived, Walker and Min were dead from what OPD assistant chief Casey Johnson characterized as “apparent gunshots” in a press conference later that day. A firearm, he said, was located at the scene. He declined to offer further details on the case, saying that the department’s homicide division would handle the investigation.

Nearly seven weeks later, we still know next to nothing about how Walker and Min died. While OPD turned down my request to speak with Johnson, it sent me a press release with the same details he laid out on October 2. Follow-up questions were met with: “There are no updates being released other than the information below.”

Bryn Walker store on Vine Street in Berkeley, California.

“I don’t know what has publicly been shared or what privately has been learned about what took place,” Salzman says carefully. Police have been silent since the brief press conference the day the bodies were discovered. But Michelle Min’s brother, Paul Min, hasn’t been quiet.

Within two days after his 63-year-old sister was found dead, Paul spoke with outlets including the LA Times and the California Post, accusing his brother-in-law of killing his wife, then himself, following a series of disastrous financial decisions that led to significant losses and a collapse in his mental state. The interviews, given so soon after the crime, suggest Paul was still in a state of shock over his loss. Walker, who was 61 when he died, was “the most honest, responsible, hardworking guy you have ever known,” Paul told the LA Times. “I loved him like a brother.” Michelle “was utterly devoted to Bryan to the very end,” Paul told the Post, “and he shot her.”

After those interviews, which were published that first weekend in October, Paul fell silent too; I made multiple efforts to arrange an interview but was ultimately unsuccessful. But according to the Post’s interview, Walker “had quietly taken out loans against their properties, and had gambled on risky options and leveraged positions,” with estimated losses of “well over $100 million.” The debt, per the LA Times story, allegedly prompted Walker to suggest that he and the Min siblings “end things”—a proposal that alarmed the Mins, but only because of its implications for Walker’s mental health. Paul didn’t see Walker as a danger: “He said the idea that Walker would or could harm them was absurd to the two of them,” reported the Times.

The Mins came to the US from Korea in 1977, settling first near Kansas City. Michelle met Walker there in the 1980s, and after the Mins’ parents chose to move to California, the siblings, and Walker, followed. In 1992 the couple opened a clothing store in Berkeley that sold goods from other makers. As time went on, they began to manufacture more and more of their own goods.

Eventually, Bryn Walker evolved into a clothing brand known for loose linen looks with an Asian-meets-Swedish flair. “Flowy, a touch eclectic, made for perhaps older women who want to mesh elegant/sophisticated with a bit of boho uniqueness,” a longtime Berkeley resident told me over email. “Women who want to look expensive but with a bit of verve.” When I described the company to one San Francisco resident as “elevated Chico’s,” I got a stern look. “You better not let any of the Bryn Walker moms at Lowell hear you say that,” she said, referencing the city’s hotly competitive public high school. “These are not humorous people.”

Bryn Walker store on Fourth Street in Berkeley, California.

According to the Post piece, Walker “had stepped aside and allowed his designer wife to control their mutual business and his eponymous fashion label,” but it’s not clear when that management change occurred. As the brand grew, it struck a chord with fashion businesses across the country—from luxury boutiques to the family-run department store chain Dillard’s. Bryn Walker also opened its own brick-and-mortar storefronts beyond Berkeley.

Many of those stores are now gone. One Bryn Walker location in Santa Monica closed prior to mid-March of 2021, while a 22-year-old outpost in Palo Alto shuttered in 2020. On the East Coast, a shop in Edgartown, on Martha’s Vineyard, went dark in 2024. A call to its shop in Vineyard Haven was met with a recorded message saying the business would be closed until further notice. That leaves just two company-owned shops, both in Berkeley, where Bryn Walker began.

One of those stores is on Berkeley’s buzzy Fourth Street, a glossy shopping destination lined with outposts of national brands like Apple, Lululemon, and Herman Miller. With items generally priced between $130–$300, it fits right into the overall ethos of that street—and Berkeley—where almost everything is spendy but not flashy; theoretically accessible, though not to those on a budget. During my recent visit to the shop, the sole staffer remained pleasant even after I identified myself as a journalist—but her tone grew firm. “It’s all still too raw,” she said of the tragedy.

I asked if, as he’d said he would in his Post interview, Paul Min had taken over management of the company following its founders’ deaths. “I don’t know about that,” she replied, before declining to speak further. I was told by another local business owner that Bryn Walker employees are actively seeking other employment; it’s unclear what will happen to the label now that its creators are gone. I tried to reach Bryn Walker management by phone and email for this story, but did not receive a response.

Emilie Raguso was one of the first journalists to report on the deaths, for her independent outlet, The Berkeley Scanner. As she began investigating, she “saw that the number of open shops was different based on where you looked,” she says. “I was getting this early inkling of what others later reported as far as the business being in trouble.”

“The writing was on the wall,” she continues, “but there was nothing explicit. It did seem like, Oh, this is not a thriving business.”

Paul’s comments to the media didn’t address the health of the business. Instead, he was focused on Walker and Michelle’s personal finances, which he alleged were laid to waste by Walker’s mismanagement. “Your spouse lied to you and lost over $100 million and you might be out on the streets,” Paul told the Post. “You might go from being one of the wealthiest people in the country to being homeless because your husband lied to you and wagered everything on crazy bets.”

According to Paul, things grew so grim for Walker that the Mins spoke about institutionalizing him. But it’s also unclear how they would have acted on that without Walker’s cooperation. California enacted its CARE Court program in 2023, more easily allowing court-ordered treatment plans for those who might pose a threat to themselves or others. But in practice, courts have been reluctant to take that drastic step, frequently rejecting petitions from those closest to the person in crisis.

Bryn Walker-Pacific Cotton store on Main Street in Vineyard Haven, Massachusetts.

Speaking with the LA Times, Paul said that in Walker and Michelle’s home, he “found a note that lists a couple of [mental health] facilities. I speculate he saw that note or somehow figured out she was going to institutionalize him, but I have no idea.”

Paul’s claim that Walker killed Michelle over snowballing financial fears isn’t out of the realm of possibility, even in a place as wealthy as the Bay Area. One year before Walker and Michelle died, almost to the day, entrepreneur Paula Truong fatally shot her husband, Thomas, and their daughters, Mackenzie and Alexandra, before hanging herself in the garage of their $2.2 million San Francisco home. Reporting found that the family had experienced a string of financial challenges, including several failed business ventures, a home foreclosure, and a number of unpaid debts.

But that was in San Francisco—a sometimes gritty city that people escape with moves to places like Panoramic Hill. “When you get up into the hills, it does feel like a world apart,” Raguso says. “It feels insulated from a lot of the more common disturbances and things that we deal with down on the flatlands.”

Salzman has lived on that hill for more than 20 years, and she’s still struggling with the notion that her neighbor might have killed his wife. “Bryan was very engaged with neighbors who were needing support that were near him,” she says, characterizing him and Michelle as “committed to the community.” But she also believes that the fear of losing wealth can drive people to desperate acts. “We see wealth as being both our greatest need and our greatest opportunity here,” she says, “and we are told that we will be happy when we consume. This is the message that we’re given everywhere we look”—especially in a region with more billionaires than anywhere else in the world.

Raguso isn’t sure why Oakland police are taking so long to announce the results of their investigation. “At some point, there would be a ruling,” she says, citing possible delays with the medical examiner’s office as a reason things haven’t been resolved. According to Salzman, the vacuum of information has inspired her to look at all her neighbors with a little more care. “Part of what I awoke to was how little I know about really what’s going on with people that I’m geographically so close to,” she says.

“I just would have loved for there to have been a way to be a part of showing up for them, even around the little things. The more people that are aware of what is happening, the more people are potentially able to heal.”

#3472. Hackers Now Want Your Browser Sessions More Than Your Passwords, but You Can Stop Them

There’s a very organized dark web supply chain that attackers use to trade in stealer logs. Russian Market has effectively replaced Genesis Market as the new storefront for black hat cybercriminals, although much of the market has also shifted to private channels on Telegram.

According to threat analysts at DarkOwl, approximately 180,000 stealer logs were sold on Russian Market in just the first half of 2025. What's more, Russian Market is a well-designed storefront that users can access even without Onion links or the Tor browser. That means anyone could go there and buy a bunch of stealer logs to start attempting account takeovers at scale.

Meanwhile, Flare Research estimates that this isn’t even close to the actual scale of the threat, because 90% of stealer logs now surface privately on Telegram. There, automated chatbots let scammers shop for stealer logs like it’s Amazon, with options to filter by country, app, and account privilege. Logs sell for anywhere between $5 and $500 a piece, depending on the estimated value of the target accounts.

The easiest way to go about this is to take a look through all your active devices and their locations in your account settings on most websites. If you see a device or location you don’t recognize, you are likely the subject of an ongoing breach. However, keep in mind that this may not always be a reliable method if you use iCloud Private Relay or a VPN. Still, it's generally best practice to log out of all active sessions every once in a while and perform a fresh login to invalidate any unauthorized sessions.

Reset the passwords on your email account, enable two-factor authentication for added protection, and sign out of all sessions before doing a fresh login. Your email inbox is the single point of entry for most attacks because that’s where most websites send their verification codes or magic links.

Sign out of all active sessions on every account that you suspect is compromised. This will log out any attackers who are currently on a hijacked browsing session.

Change your passwords on every platform in order of priority. Start with banking websites, cloud storage providers, and password managers first.

Look through each compromised account’s third-party integrations and app permissions. Revoke access if you can’t recognize an app, or it looks suspicious. Also make sure to rotate any API keys that you’re currently using, since those may have been compromised as well.

But while the initiative has already been open-sourced, no other major online provider has begun offering native support for it as of this article. That means DBSC’s security benefits are limited to Google services like Gmail and Docs, Chrome for Windows, and third-party websites that offer single sign-on (SSO) options for your Google account. We might see a wider rollout in the near future, though.
