#3453. The Nightingale First Look: Dakota and Elle Fanning on Their Long-Awaited First Film as Sisters

When I spoke to Dakota and Elle Fanning last fall, they pondered what it would be like to work and live together while making The Nightingale, the film adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s best-selling novel about French sisters in Nazi-occupied France. It marks the siblings’ first time acting opposite each other onscreen. “We’ve literally never done a scene together, ever,” Dakota said then, as Elle wondered if she’d get through their first take without breaking character: “Am I going to laugh? Better to get it out of your system now.”

Now, more than a year later, the Fanning sisters tell me they needn’t have worried. “It was nerve-wracking to think, ‘How is this going to feel?’” says Dakota, who’s in New York to shoot an Apple TV series opposite Elle’s former Sentimental Value co-star Stellan Skarsgard. “Our way of processing things that we’re both nervous about is to just not talk about it in an effort to downplay what could go wrong or be strange. So that’s what we did—and it was the easiest thing in the world. We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”

Hollywood has long been plotting to get the Fanning sisters in the same movie—and not as different versions of the same character, as they played in Dakota’s 2001 feature debut, I Am Sam. They were in talks to colead My Sister’s Keeper, a 2009 tearjerker about a young girl conceived to become a marrow donor for her gravely ill sister, but stepped away from it because Dakota didn’t want to shave her head. (Sofia Vassilieva and Abigail Breslin ended up in the movie.) Plus, as Dakota previously told me, she and Elle acting together at that age “would’ve been gimmicky.”

Now, the Fannings say they felt ready to streamline their singular talents into one special project. “We never shied away from being together because we are so close, but we both feel properly established on our own,” says Dakota. “So getting to do things together, together, together is a real joy.”

The Nightingale, which hits theaters on March 19, 2027, follows guarded older sibling Vianne, who urges caution when dealing with the Germans but later shields Jewish children in her home—and rebellious younger sister Isabelle, who joins the French Resistance and becomes a target of the Nazis. “What I love about it is it’s two women fighting, resisting,” Elle previously told VF. “One in a louder way, one in a quiet way.”

Dakota and Elle were bound for preproduction in Budapest on The Nightingale as the pandemic hit in March 2020. “It has been a long time coming,” says Hannah, the book’s author. “These two young women have been attached to this project and been passionate about it for a very long time,” Hannah tells VF. “As the author, to have two female partners who were as dedicated to bringing this novel to screen in the way I saw it as well, felt like a remarkable gift.”

Hannah, whose 2008 novel Firefly Lane was later adapted into a Netflix series starring Katherine Heigl and Sarah Chalke, says she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her own books for the screen. “I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.” But she was a part of the script development process for The Nightingale with screenwriter Dana Stevens from the very start. “Nightingale has always been a very special book for me,” says Hannah. “And more importantly, it’s a very special book for my readers.”

When the project was revived, the Fannings returned not only as stars, but producers through their Lewellen Pictures production banner. Filmmaker Michael Morris, fresh off the fourth Bridget Jones movie, stepped in to replace their original director, French actor Mélanie Laurent. Just as Bridget Jones was an opportunity to make a film about grief under the guise of romantic comedy, Morris saw The Nightingale as his chance to explore sisterhood through a sweeping World War II epic. “I saw these two women, how they exist independently in the world as complimentary creatures,” says the director, who is also father to three daughters. “They are built from the same building blocks, but they’ve gone different ways.”

Morris clocked a similar dynamic between his leads. “Elle is immediately outgoing and loud and can feel super funny making fun of herself. Dakota has all those qualities too, but can sometimes be very focused and funny in a sort of sly, quieter way,” he explains. “They fill up the spaces that the other one leaves for each other, like all really good siblings. I met with Dakota, and then I met with Elle, and by the end of the Elle meeting, I was like, ‘I totally understand this film.’”

Of the more than 11 million copies of The Nightingale that have been sold worldwide, perhaps the most valuable belongs to Elle and Dakota’s grandmother, who after reading the 2015 historical novel told her granddaughters that they would be perfect for the parts of Isabelle and Vianne. “Vianne shows her love through nurture and cooking and taking care of a home. Elle’s character, Isabelle, is the more obviously daring one that runs towards danger and adventure,” says Dakota. “I do think that we are truly probably the people to play these roles because we deeply understand that dynamic. We inhabit some of the same qualities.”

Although presented with separate drivers at the start of production, Elle and Dakota rode to set for their joint scenes in the same car. “[The characters] are apart a lot of the time, so when we had scenes that were together, those were treated with a lot of care,” says Elle, speaking backstage from Today, where she promoted her role as a young Effie Trinket in The Hunger Games prequel. “Because it’s quite powerful to finally see them united and to see us on screen together.”

Their director says because Elle and Dakota had never acted opposite one another, they brought a vibrant, kinetic energy to each shared scene—an offering that Morris took seriously as the filmmaker to capture it. “We’re talking about women who are barely 30 who have been working at the highest level for 25 years. A quarter of a century spent on sets of really wonderful projects,” he explains. “So you have all this experience that they have that they can bring to bear in a moment. It’s like watching someone who’s incredibly talented at athletics. They look and function like normal people, and then you kick a football at them and they suddenly do incredible things. Like, ‘Whoa, where did that come from?’”

The Fannings left it all out on the field—and tried not to bring work home into their shared living space. “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” says Elle. “And also knowing that we’re representing these women from that time,” including Andrée de Jongh, a Belgian woman who was helping downed airmen escape from France during World War II, whose story Hannah says helped inspire her original novel. “Because there’s so much brain power [used] on set,” says Elle, at the end of each day “you have to just recharge and eat Thai food.”

The sisters’ downtime involved a steady stream of true-crime and Real Housewives, as well as Dakota’s first full-fledged watch of Elle’s Emmy-nominated Apple TV series Margo’s Got Money Troubles, released in the thick of The Nightingale’s filming schedule. “So what we do,” says Dakota, “my mom does this too, is when any of us has something that’s out, she turns on every TV in the house and leaves it playing, as she says, ‘For the views.’” Elle and Dakota each laugh, shaking their heads a little. “So I was doing that with Margo,” Dakota recalls. “I’d have it going on my iPad and my phone when they were sitting there charging. For the views.”

But they couldn’t block out their day jobs entirely. When Dakota had a day off, she, like her character Vianne, found herself picking up after her younger sister while she worked. “Her bed in the morning is like a tornado has run through it,” says Dakota. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’”

“It’s art imitating life,” says Elle, “because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed too.” By the end of the shoot, says Dakota, “it became a routine. I always made her bed like that when I could.”

But the Fannings were fully aligned on the casting of their fictional father, calling Oscar winner Mark Rylance their “dream casting,” from the beginning. “I always say he has twinkly eyes,” Elle explains. “We all know what an incredible actor he is, but to see it up close and get to act opposite that—it was really, really powerful.” Adds Dakota, “As a person and as an actor, you just feel his emotions and soul and heart on his fingertips [even] when he shakes your hand.”

Morris thinks of Rylance’s character, Julien, an emotionally stunted World War I veteran, as the “third axis of a triangle—but he’s not just binding them together as sisters, he’s also tearing them apart because he’s not a healthy role model for most of their lives,” says the filmmaker. “Because Mark can be wonderfully lovable, we talked about what is it not to lean on that? What is it to be a bad parent? What is it to neglect? And it’s painful, but he doesn’t hide from the flaws of his character. He doesn’t try to make you love him.”

The rest of the ensemble cast includes up-and-comers like Unorthodox breakout Shira Haas, All Quiet on the Western Front star Albrecht Schuch, and Civil War’s Edmund Donovan as Gaëtan, a communist resistance fighter and love interest for Elle’s character, Isabelle. The younger Fanning also enlisted a few of her co-stars on the Emmy-nominated Hulu series The Great for the film, including Douglas Hodge and Gwilym Lee, who plays Antoine, the soldier husband of Dakota’s character, Vianne. But “this is not a war movie,” Morris insists. “We are telling the story of real people from the POV of two young women living at the time. They’re not glued in on the grand sweep of history. They’re just living, trying to do the best they can. It’s not about the politics of the time, it’s about what you do about it. It’s a very contemporary film because I don’t know anyone who hasn't grown up in a time when there isn’t something to get active about.”

Hannah hopes that the film version of her novel will shed light on the fact that “so many of women’s important historical stories have been lost or discounted,” adding, “Isabelle and Vianne, and in fact, many of the characters in this book risk their lives on a daily basis to fight for what they believe is right. And that’s a really important message at any time, now and throughout history.”

It wasn’t until their final week shooting the hotly-anticipated adaptation that the Fannings got into something approaching a fight—while filming one of their favorite moments from the book, no less. “It really had nothing to do with the scene,” Dakota tells VF. “It was literally because we were on a couch that was too small for both of us. Elle had the comfortable position and I was hanging off one side, uncomfortable and hot. And the way that I saw it is you are pushing me off.”

“Sabotage!” Elle interjects, wiping her morning-show makeup off mid-call with a mischievous grin. “I was like, ‘You’re sweating! Get this leg off of me.’ And Elle was like, ‘Stop talking to me.’ It was like a miniature explosion,” Dakota recalls with a laugh. “We both looked over at the crew and they were grinning from ear-to-ear, like, ‘Finally, there it is.’ It was the closest thing that they had seen to a little disgruntledness from both of us.”

That scene was also a favorite for Morris, who removed much of the script’s dialogue to focus on the dynamic between the sisters, both real and fictional. “Seeing these two women bring their entire life history as sisters to the moment, putting them that close together on this tiny couch, gave them no option but to be really close,” says Morris, who realized, “Oh, we need almost no words at all to tell the scene. Elle Fanning, Dakota Fanning, playing these sisters, brings us so much that we can just be there with them.”

Hannah has yet to see the finished film, but is most eager to watch “the moment where Isabelle grabs her long braid and cuts her hair off in front of the Nazi officer to show her defiance, and her sister’s horror that she would be impulsive enough to do something like that and put them all in danger,” she tells VF. “I’m a little afraid to see the fullness of my vision through this film and how it will impact me. I have a feeling that I’m going to be crying like everybody else.”

Nerves aside, Hannah is optimistic about the finished product after visiting The Nightingale set, where she walked through her characters’ childhood home, built from scratch, as dictated in the pages of her novel. “Down to the smallest detail, their vision was this magnification of my vision. Everything looked exactly as I had pictured it, and my research had defined it. Then to see Elle and Mark Rylance bring these characters to life in a way that even goes beyond what I am able to imagine was…” she trails off. “I guess the only word I can use really is magical.”

To hear the Fannings tell it, the experience was similarly profound. “Of course, we visit each other on sets and I’ve seen her work,” says Elle, “but it’s very different to be looking at each other in front of a camera. It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer. Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’”

“But we did really savor it,” Dakota replies. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything,” she says, giving her sister a meaningful glance across the Zoom screen. “That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.”

#3452. After Gilligan's Island, Jim Backus Appeared In This 1977 Disney Cult Classic

"Gilligan's Island" came to an end after three seasons in 1967, and while he reprised the role of Thurston Howell III in two animated "Gilligan's Island" spin-offs and three TV continuation movies, Jim Backus found time for plenty of other projects. That included two collaborations with director Don Chaffey.

The first of these saw Chaffey, of "Jason and the Argonauts" fame, direct Backus in the 1977 live action/animation hybrid "Pete's Dragon." /Film previously dubbed "Pete's Dragon" a fascinating and surprisingly mean Disney oddity, and that's largely true — though watching this movie as a kid I don't recall being particularly struck by the meanness of it. Looking back, however, there were certainly some surprisingly dark moments in the film, including the opening musical number in which a gang of hillbillies sing enthusiastically about recapturing their escaped child slave and "tying him screaming to a railroad track."

Disney was going through a transitional phase at the time, during which things just seemed to get a little more grim than usual. "Pete's Dragon" debuted the same year as another Disney movie with some dreary overtones: "The Rescuers." But the former was particularly odd for combining its songs about child slavery with a wholesome throwback musical vibe and a lovable cartoon dragon overlaid on live-action scenes. It resulted in a film that seemed simultaneously ahead of its time technically and yet felt like one big anachronism in a year that also gave us two of the greatest sci-fi movies of all time. Having Thurston Howell pop up just added to the disorientation, even if Backus was only in a few scenes.

"Pete's Dragon" stars Sean Marshall as young orphan Pete, who escapes from the aforementioned hillbillies, the Gogans, with the help of his invisible dragon friend, Elliott. Pete manages to avoid being tied screaming to the railroad tracks and makes it to the Maine fishing village of Passamaquoddy. There, he meets lighthouse keeper Lampie (Mickey Rooney), and his kind adult daughter Nora, (Helen Reddy), who take in Pete and become the loving family he's always needed.

Meanwhile, traveling snake oil salesman Doc Terminus (Jim Dale) and his assistant Hoagy (Red Buttons) arrive in Passamaquoddy and win over the townspeople with their grift. When Dale's villain discovers the existence of Elliott, however, he becomes obsessed with capturing the beast to concoct new tonics. Soon, the Gogans also arrive to claim Pete, before forming an alliance with Terminus to recapture both their former child slave and Elliott.

Jim Backus appears in a few brief scenes as the Mayor of Passamaquoddy, who twice finds himself the victim of an invisible Elliot's antics. Backus isn't in the film much, but does a decent job with the physical comedy of his scenes, recalling moments from his "Gilligan's Island" years. The actor previously lent his voice talents, honed over several decades of playing one of animation's most famous characters, Mr. Magoo, to the 1951 Disney animated short "Plutopia" and later played Timothy Forsythe in the 1972 live-action Disney comedy "Now You See Him, Now You Don't." The Mayor in "Pete's Dragon" was his final Disney role — though he was referenced in Disney's attempt to revive Mr. Magoo with a live action update that Roger Ebert called "transcendently bad." Happily, the same can't be said for "Pete's Dragon," even if it has gone mostly overlooked.

Originally conceived as an episode of "Walt Disney's Disneyland" back in the mid-'50s, "Pete's Dragon" was scrapped before eventually being revisited in the mid-'70s. By this time, pop culture looked a lot different than two decades prior. 1977 was, of course, the year a little movie titled "Star Wars" debuted, as well as Steven Spielberg's "Close Encounters of the Third Kind."

Released on November 3, 1977, "Pete's Dragon," a throwback musical set in early 1900s Maine and shot on the Disney backlot, found itself sandwiched between two of the best sci-fi movies of all time. "Star Wars" and "Close Encounters" were both symbolic of mass audiences' changing tastes as sci-fi came to rule the world. As such, "Pete's Dragon" went mostly overlooked.

That is, the film has been mostly overlooked since its release. In 1977 it actually made Disney a decent profit, earning $35.4 million upon its 1977 debut and a further $4.1million when it was re-released in 1984. On a $10 million budget, that ain't bad. The movie also earned two Oscar nominations, one for musical scoring and another for original song. Still, "Pete's Dragon" never became a Disney classic, which is a shame because I, and I'm sure others, were enchanted by it as a kid.

Meanwhile, Jim Backus went on to collaborate with Don Chaffey a second time in the 1979 sci-fi comedy "C.H.O.M.P.S. " It, too went mostly overlooked. Some 37 years later in 2016, we got a "Pete's Dragon" remake which was similarly underrated and is a must-watch for "How to Train your Dragon" fans. But the original is such a charming little oddity that it could never truly be outdone. If you fancy checking it out, the film is available to watch on Disney+.

#3451. The GTA 6 Review

Rockstar’s magnum opus searches for love and catharsis in desperate times — and finds them

Who gets to break the rules in America? A cryptobro living off of financial scams. A girlboss CEO who turns feminine vulnerability into a pyramid scheme. A cop who shoots a civilian in the face and walks away scot-free. It’s an exclusive club of societally acceptable grifters and killers, and Lucia Caminos’ name isn’t on the VIP list.

When we first meet the co-star of Grand Theft Auto 6, she’s scraping the bottom of the cultural barrel. She’s a lowly street rat. The only person who seems to give a damn about her is Jason Duval, another small-time crook who connects with her during a star-crossed carjacking turned meet-cute. It doesn’t take long for the law to interrupt her rom-com dreams, landing her in prison with other low-tier riffraff crammed together like sheep in a pen.

When Lucia is finally set free, it’s not because society has decided that this financially desperate Latina has earned a second chance. It’s because of an overcrowding crisis at the jail.

In a sprawling satirical sandbox filled with loudmouth radio DJs and over-the-top conservative cartoons, it’s the sharpest stab GTA 6 lands on American culture. Justice is big business in the Florida-inspired state of Leonida, and people like Lucia are products to be cycled in and out of a flawed system. All the while, the real criminal masterminds of Leonida trash their penthouses into the wee morning hours.

Lucia’s unjust origin story is the key to understanding and embracing GTA 6’s tantalizing power fantasy, panicked parents and politicians be damned. Rockstar Games’ astonishing open-world adventure, the most impossibly grand and expensive video game that may ever exist, doesn’t just generate its morbid pleasure from cop-killing sprees and armed robberies; that comes from living in a reactive place governed by intricate rules that beg to be bent and busted. If you can learn to outmaneuver police helicopters and escape with duffel bags full of unmarked bills, you’ll be rewarded with a small taste of the law-breaking freedom that’s only offered to a certain class of crook in America.

It’s no wonder that, after decades of moral panic, GTA once again earns its title as public enemy #1 — only this time, Rockstar accomplishes that less through bloodshed and more with an empathetic love story built for an era of stark economic uncertainty. It’s a bold choice, considering the series’ cold-blooded reputation, but it’s also what makes GTA 6 one of Rockstar’s finest games to date.

Following an opening prologue that ends with Lucia behind bars, the story really kicks off as her sentence is winding down. Jason, now living in a dilapidated shack in the Keys, has found a modest living doing odd jobs for Brian, an old-timer who has mastered the art of laying low far outside of Vice City. When Jason receives word that Lucia is getting an early release, it lights a fire under him to get his house in order so that the lovers can have a chance at a normal life. Key word: normal.

The opening chapter, filled with low-level crimes and mundane roof-patching missions, makes for a strong introduction to a story about a couple scraping by. Whereas some GTA games explicitly focus on the myth of the American Dream, following wannabe kingpins who can’t get enough money and power, Jason and Lucia’s motivations are more down to Earth. The duo’s ultimate goal is to earn enough cash to skip town and support one another. While you can spend your riches on guns and designer clothing, your big-picture aim is to fill up a savings account via the in-game BuckMe cash app. That’s the real dream.

It’s a more human GTA story that’s sold by Jason and Lucia. Both characters get equal screen time during the campaign, and both are compelling leads in their own way. Jason is a veteran, a detail that’s never deeply explored, but one that subtly establishes him as a person who has been left behind. Why is he living in a leaking shack and reduced to working shady gigs while patriotic right-wing media dominates Leonida’s radio waves and TV stations? There’s a lingering sense that he’s been used and tossed aside on the literal outskirts of America.

Jason is also a true himbo: a monotone musclehead who reveals his heart of gold early on when quietly obsessing over home renovation tasks once he learns Lucia is getting out. He has the energy of a young Channing Tatum, with charm and sincerity always poking through his tough guy persona. Jason also works as the perfect straight man for the oddball rat race that is Leonida. He’s just as confused as you are when a stranger escapes a car crash and decides to hop back into the burning vehicle to ensure he gets a bigger insurance payout. The shit people will do for money in this town.

But Lucia is the real star of the power couple. She’s unapologetically brash, and has no reservations about getting back to a life of crime after getting out of prison. That can make her seem one-dimensional at first, but it’s grounded in a real anxiety that crops up between her snarkiest one-liners. A key flashback shows her struggling to make ends meet as a ride-share driver, weathering racist abuse from passengers who in turn tank her rating. There’s a sense that she’s hit a dead end in a world that hates her; even an app is rigged against her. She sees little choice but to accept risky jobs in hope that she can put even $500 into her bank account. The shit this town makes us do for money.

Leonida is full of natural predators that circle its swamps like hungry alligators.

The central story, which has the rhythm of a five-season prestige TV series, sees the couple graduating to bigger crimes and even bigger apartments as they move throughout the state. Small gigs in the Keys soon give way to harmless carjackings upstate, and then to tense bank robberies in Vice City’s urban core. While there are some thrilling heists along the way that require meticulous planning across multiple missions, the story can sag when it’s inventing elaborate excuses to tutorialize features, reposition Jason and Lucia around the map, and introduce last-minute villains in time for its rushed final stretch. Instead, its most effective moments come in all the quiet conversations that happen between bank jobs, where Jason and Lucia trade insecurities about the viability of their shared future in a place like Leonida.

That feeling does not exist in a cultural vacuum. In true South Park fashion, Rockstar takes as many potshots as it can at the current state of American culture. It plays out like a damning, if sometimes dated, retrospective of the past decade — you could subtitle it “I Hate the 2020s.” Jason finds himself tangled up in a crypto scam. Lucia stumbles into a multi-level marketing scheme disguised as a noble women’s wellness business. Flip on a radio, and you might catch the all-too familiar sounds of a conservative whining about trans athletes in school sports, only to reveal that he’s a little too eager to "protect" young girls, if you catch my drift. Leonida is full of natural predators that circle its swamps like hungry alligators.

That’s the environment that our antiheroes find themselves sinking in while the bastards swim. Petty theft will earn someone like Lucia an immediate trip to jail, but everyone else appears to be getting away with much worse. Through its satirical mirror, GTA 6 questions why some people need to play by the rules while others don’t. (You can even see that reflected in the game’s own comedic targets: Rockstar goes out of its way to avoid lampooning powerful political figures like Donald Trump, but it’s not shy about dunking on rural rednecks and people living in the slums, struggling with substance use disorders.)

It doesn’t always feel like there’s much an individual can do to topple structural inequities in real life. But in a safe digital playground like this? You can start to understand the inherent appeal of blowing off steam in GTA 6’s punching-bag world.

While there’s a lot to unpack in this downright enormous game, the basic catharsis of GTA remains unchanged here. When you’re not working through story missions filled with third-person shootouts and car chases pulled straight from a Hollywood movie, you’re free to cause as much chaos as you want in Leonida. Jack a car, mug a pedestrian at gunpoint, rob a gas station — live your criminal fantasies as long as you can before the police rain on your parade. Decades after it first stirred moral panic, GTA’s appeal remains its unmatched ability to let players see just how much they can get away with as you test your relationship to authority.

Video games are a perfect avenue for that because they’re built on rules. You can only jump this high. You can’t access this area until you’ve found the right key. Killing this character will result in this consequence. Every time you enter a new world, your immediate task is to learn the law of the land. Your second, and more fun, task becomes figuring out how and when to break those laws. GTA 6’s greatest strength is that it offers an entire nation of laws. They spill out from countless criss-crossing systems that require you to keep your head on a swivel at all times.

Steal a car without scanning it first with a phone app that reveals its security system, and you might find yourself panicking when an unseen tracker starts beeping. Fail to find someone hiding in a back room during an attempted bank heist? They’ll have enough time to get free and trigger an alarm. Robberies are an especially strong addition to GTA 6 in that respect — not just because they let you explore interior spaces, but because they require you to get every detail right. You need to act quickly to compel guards to drop their guns, threaten cashiers to hand over safe codes, or destroy any security camera footage hiding in a server room. There are so many ways you can screw up unexpectedly, but that makes it all the more satisfying when you pull off a clean getaway just before the cops pull up to the scene of the crime.

Even GTA’s signature wanted system requires much more of your attention now, as police are now able to track your car, face, and outfit if someone sees you. Listen to the cops on your scanner, and you’ll hear them sharing the vehicle and outfit you were spotted in, or even your build. You’re not even fully out of the woods when you outrun the fuzz, as you’ll leave a temporary heat level in the area you committed a crime as cops continue to look for you. My first three-star chase was a 30-minute cat-and-mouse game that had me abandoning vehicles and scrambling over fences to get away. Just when I thought I was safe after having thrown on a hat and glasses, the chase began again once a passing cop car got a look at me for a moment too long.

All of this is different for a GTA game that is chasing a certain level of hyperrealism. Here, Rockstar very much builds on the groundwork it laid in 2018’s laborious Red Dead Redemption 2. For instance, you can build muscle by following a strict workout routine that requires you to do a certain number of reps within a set time period, and even build rests into your training regiment. If you want to steal a locked car without smashing the window and setting off an alarm, you’ll need to use a slim jim to carefully pick the lock. While that attention to detail could often feel tiresome in the slow-paced world of Red Dead, everything moves mercifully faster here, which makes sense considering that you’re barreling around town in sports cars instead of plodding down dusty roads on horseback.

Still, it takes some adjusting to. In my first sessions, I found myself almost scared to do anything I wouldn’t do in real life. Something about the photorealistic visuals has changed my usual GTA brain chemistry; I was suddenly stopping at traffic lights and refusing to cut in front of cars. But that would end up being a functional anxiety. Every session offered another opportunity to see what rules I could bend. Broken traffic laws led to quiet stick-ups in isolated pawn shops led to full-scale assaults on Leonida’s most well-guarded banks. Progression like this is baked into a story of escalating crimes, but it’s also built into the very psychology of GTA 6.

It’s easy to get reductive when discussing the broad appeal of GTA. Many would have you believe that its popularity is a symptom of a sick society that glorifies crime and violence. Maybe there’s some truth to that, but it doesn’t get to the heart of the series. Its joy has more in common with a kid screwing around in class as much as they can without landing in detention. When you possess little power in the world, there’s a pleasure in getting to push what buttons you can. (Even calling out sick from work to play GTA 6 on launch day can be seen as workers exercising the tiniest bit of institutional rebellion.) That’s made all the more powerful in this story, with these characters, within this laundry list of intricate laws.

None of this would matter much if the world wasn’t worth living in, but Leonida makes for the perfect setting. An enormous map that has been in the works since 2015, as Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson told Polygon in an interview last week, GTA 6’s take on Florida packs an entire state’s worth of scenic landscapes and local eccentrics into one coherent place. While returning players might be most excited to spend time in the glitzy Vice City, that’s arguably the least interesting location in the game.

In the south, you have the Leonida Keys. Almost designed with the same tutorial zone philosophy underpinning Breath of the Wild’s Great Plateau, it perfectly captures the compact, distant nature of the real Florida Keys. It feels like you’re in a world physically detached from the state, where you don’t have a lot of avenues for escape if you go on a murder spree. It’s the perfect place to learn the rules of the road before things open up the further north you get. That stands in contrast to the very top of the state, a wide open rural landscape that’s built for hunters and hikers (and, unlike IRL Florida, actually features topography of differing elevations). Some of my favorite moments of the game so far have simply come from biking around mountains and stumbling into off-road racetracks and crumbling ruins.

It’s the rare open-world game that feels a mile wide and a mile deep.

There’s a lot to take in, especially considering how much work Rockstar puts into locking down the right aesthetics. The world itself is astoundingly detailed, with everything from a crowded strip club to a stray island off in the water feeling like it was hand designed and placed with purpose. That comes at the expense of peak performance, as GTA 6 runs at 30 frames per second with some dips when police chases hit the five-star mark. But that’s a negligible impact on the overall experience, given how smoothly it runs most of the time. (I played GTA 6 on a PS5 Pro.) And it’s a fair trade for a world that deserves its own line of postcards.

Driving around it is an auditory delight too, as GTA 6 features a soundtrack so large and diverse that you have to wonder if half of the budget went to music licensing. Metallica and Slayer are there for the metalheads, Charli XCX and Chappell Roan for the modern pop aficionados, and a whole lot of Trick Daddy and Juvenile for those who want to pay respects to the greats of the Dirty South rap scene. All of is spread between satirical commercials and radio shows that clue you into Leonida’s political climate as you drive. (Though be prepared to hear a lot of low-hanging dick jokes; GTA 6’s writers lean hard on cocks as a comedic crutch.) Every little artistic touch helps bring Leonida to life beyond its landmarks.

While there’s plenty to see and hear, I’m more impressed with how much of the world doesn’t feel constructed for players to explore. I occasionally drive by the kind of roadside construction areas that you pass by while on the highway. I don’t think much of them in real life; that’s not an area that I need to pull over and see! GTA 6 mirrors that experience, loading the world with so many mundane sights that ground the world in realism. You can go to them, of course. You might even find a collectible trading card or a wad of cash there. But there’s always a sense that life is happening in Leonida, even when you’re not there.

The best example is in how Jason and Lucia stumble into happenings in Leonida. While the map is filled with markers indicating main story quests, robbery locations, and other activities of note, many other things can just happen out of nowhere. Entire side quests can be discovered by noticing a guy drunkenly barreling down the highway on a tractor, or following the voice of a man looking for his lost cow. Those missable moments often hide the best quests in GTA 6 and imbue the world with more personality than you can imagine.

Other world events aren’t there to kick off missions at all. In one session, I heard the sound of police sirens and followed them downside road to find the cops surrounding a garage. A woman emerged and revealed that she was making kitty litter in there, not drugs. That wasn’t tied to a quest, nor did it have any story implications or rewards tied to it. It’s just a thing that I happened to catch. I’ve similarly seen plane crashes in the distance, watched the cops get into a standoff with a furry, and passed under a bridge as a group of troublemakers above threw tires down on the cars below. Sometimes I insert myself into those situations. (I sure gave those rabble-rousers a talking-to.) Other times, I decide it’s just not my business. The fact that I can make that choice adds a remarkable level of depth to Leonida, a place where you’re always reminded that Jason and Lucia aren’t the only two people who are up to some shit. Everyone is off on their own hustle.

That barely begins to cover what you can experience in Leonida. There are shooting ranges, golf courses, basketball hoops, meditation spots, diving expeditions, stunt jumps, drone-flying challenges, scannable landmarks, and more collectibles than you can imagine. Hell, there are multiple street racing leagues that will make you feel like you’re playing Forza Horizon 6 as streets get repurposed into natural circuits. There’s even an extensive vehicle modification system to allow you to fine-tune cars to your liking. It’s the rare open-world game that feels a mile wide and a mile deep.

What’s surprising about all of that is that it somehow avoids feeling totally overwhelming. Maybe it’s just because there’s so much to do that it’s easy to accept from the jump that you will likely never see it all, but I haven’t felt a compulsion to do anything in GTA 6. Everything is just another potential avenue to make money in a world where stable employment isn’t an option for Jason and Lucia. Want to earn a living fencing cars? You could just do that. Feel like busting up meth labs and selling the goods instead? You’ll have plenty of opportunities. The ultimate power of GTA 6 is that you have the freedom to pick your poison and carve out your own life in Leonida. Why shouldn’t Lucia have that privilege that’s afforded to everyone around her?

So, you can break all the rules in GTA 6. You can do more crimes than ever before. You can kill seabirds and throw them at people. You can amass a fortune on mounds of stolen cocaine and unmarked bills. So what?

That’s an important question not just for finding value in a video game that you could probably play for a decade, but in real life too. One of my deepest daily anxieties comes when I think too hard about existing in an employment battle royale. I know that I need a job to get the money to live, but what’s the point? Aren’t I just busting my ass for the privilege of waking up another day and busting my ass again? I spiral over it constantly; the eat-work-sleep cycle becomes claustrophobic the more I focus so tightly on it that I can no longer see its endpoint. (I imagine that Rockstar’s own staff may be grappling with similar feelings right now, as they are currently fighting to unionize.) It’s easy to lose your hope, motivation, or sense of self when you don’t have something to fight for.

GTA 6’s secret weapon for addressing that malaise comes back to Jason and Lucia. A video game starring a couple has a lot of upsides on a pure design level, and Rockstar takes full advantage of that dynamic. You can freely swap between characters outside of some early story stretches, allowing you to dress up and manage two heroes with distinct personalities. Some missions even have you flipping between them during dramatic set pieces, letting you cover yourself when you wind up pinned down during a tense shootout. When you’re about to do a bank robbery, you can invite your partner to the spot and go in together to ensure you can carry more bags and cover your vulnerabilities. When you leave, you can even command one character to head off and fence the spoils instead of lugging it back to a buyer manually. All of these scenarios allow you to think more strategically about how you pull off crimes, and how you spend your time.

But what’s more effective is how the two can interact when they’re not on the job. GTA 6’s real hero feature is an optional relationship system that allows you to create a romantic bond between Jason and Lucia. When I’m playing as one character, for instance, I can pull out my phone and call or text my partner. (You can text and drive, but be prepared to learn why you should never do that in real life.) That can be just to check in and see how they’re doing, or to invite them to come hang out on a whim. They’ll arrive either in their own car or a ride-share a few moments later, and you’ll find yourself on an impromptu date.

The benefits of GTA 6’s activity-filled world and systems-heavy design reveal themselves in those tender moments. One time, I took Lucia out for a round of mini-golf. Another time, I invited her out to the club and spent hundreds of dollars on champagne for us as we danced together. At any point, you can pull up a menu that allows you to strike up a conversation, flirt, or even hold hands. The two can also fall into natural conversations while hanging out. One time while driving, a country song came on the radio. Lucia started talking about how she thought country music was a big joke growing up, prompting a sweet little exchange between the couple as they chatted about the genre. It felt like a real conversation that would come up with your partner during a road trip.

I already know the wild story moments that GTA 6 will be widely remembered for — there are some fantastic ones involving a pulse-pounding airport caper and an accidental porn set misadventure. But I don’t think I’ll remember many of the repetitive drive-and-shoot chases that clog up a long story that recycles the same ideas a few too many times. Instead, it’s the intimate interactions that stick with me now. One of my favorite moments in the entire game didn’t happen during a mission or cutscene at all. It was when I woke up one morning to find Lucia standing on the balcony of our apartment. I walked up behind her, gave her a kiss, and held her in silence as we looked out across the beach below. I let it play out as long as I could before heading out for another day of blood and bullets.

That’s the so what. Through Jason and Lucia’s genuine chemistry, GTA 6 gives you a better reason to work through Leonida’s daily grind. Yes, there’s always another bank to rob or car to steal, but that’s not the reason you wake up in the morning. It’s to prove that love can survive in a cruel culture that tries so hard to beat it out of people. So be it if you have to play dirty to keep pace with the cold-hearted crooks who make their fortune from someone else’s pain. It shouldn’t be this hard to settle down with your lover and enjoy a sunset together in the rotten social climate that Rockstar has been eager to lampoon for decades at this point.

People will hem and haw about Grand Theft Auto’s purported glamorization of lawlessness. They always have; they always will. But it will be different this time. GTA 6’s empathy is bound to be the most controversial thing about it.

Grand Theft Auto 6 will be released Nov. 19 on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. The game was reviewed on PlayStation 5 Pro using a prerelease download code provided by Rockstar Games. You can find additional information about Polygon’s ethics policy here.

#3449. 43 Years Later, A Christmas Story's Most Famous Line Remains The Best Christmas Movie Quote

Feeling that chill in the air, the rising number of Oscars-hopeful movie releases in theaters, and the unmistakable threat promise of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas is You" playing in every department store you enter for the foreseeable future? Yep, you know what that means: The holiday season is officially upon us and we're positively giddy with Yuletide cheer. Of course, we're even more excited about finally having an excuse to pop on our favorite films and celebrate the festivities properly.

For those of us who practically grew up on one particular classic, that involves ringing in the holidays with "A Christmas Story," arguably the most quintessential Christmas movie of them all. There are approximately a hundred different reasons why this of all movies captures the essence of the season the most — or, more accurately, the childlike wonder and innocence we all used to have come November of every single year. The seemingly endless wait for school to end and the fun to begin. The breathless anticipation every time our parents left the house for some clandestine gift shopping. The snowball fights and snow days and warm evenings by the fire, for those of us fortunate enough to live in more wintry climates.

"A Christmas Story" takes all those evocative feelings and wraps them inside a snow globe of nostalgia ... with a little commentary on crass commercialism, nuclear family dynamics, and some good ol' fashioned childhood bullying thrown in for good measure. Forty three years later, it's a pop-culture staple that endures. And one particular quote about a certain Red Ryder BB gun goes a long way towards explaining why.

"You'll shoot your eye out." — Ralph's mother.

Ah, the life-and-death stakes of being a child during the holidays. Every single item on our list is a must-have present or the world will end forever. Each day is fraught with the most impossible homework assignments we need to finish before we can have fun with friends. And every impulsive misstep or moment of misbehavior comes with the possibility of turning Santa Claus himself against us. For Ralphie (Peter Billingsley), the precocious 9-year-old boy living in 1940s Indiana retelling the events of "A Christmas Story" to us as an adult (narrated by Jean Shepherd), it all comes down to those five crushing words that destroy all his holiday hopes in one fell swoop.

"You'll shoot your eye out," of course, refers to his mother's (Melinda Dillon) appalled reaction to the #1 item on his Christmas list: an Official Red Ryder Carbine-Action 200-Shot Range Model Air Rifle with a compass in the stock and a sundial, to put it plainly. It's his white whale, the forbidden fruit that torments and dazzles poor Ralphie for the entirety of the film's runtime. And when he finally works up the nerve to ask his mom for her blessing, well, she sensibly points out exactly what could go wrong with such a violent "toy."

It's a perfect encapsulation of the beating heart of "A Christmas Story" and why multiple generations have gravitated towards this movie. It brings us right back to that indescribable feeling of being eight or nine or 10, with an entire world of possibility ahead ... if only the adults would let us free. After countless re-watches, well, the hilarious (and predictable) punchline proves kids don't always know best, after all.

#3448. 'GTA 6' Runs Best on This Console

Grand Theft Auto 6 might just be the most anticipated game of all time. It's been 13 years since Rockstar dropped GTA 5, and after years of rumors, leaks, and official announcements, the sixth mainstream installment in the series is nearly here. In fact, anyone who pre-ordered the game digitally can now pre-load it onto their console, if you want to ensure you're ready to play the second the game comes out.

Now, few of us will buy a game console specifically for GTA 6—unless you don't already have a current-generation PlayStation or Xbox. (The PC version of the game isn't expected until at least early 2027.) But, as it turns out, there's one specific console that can run GTA 6 better than the rest.

Rockstar confirmed as much in a post on Tuesday, which was meant to spread the news about pre-loading the game. But, interestingly, it spurred a discussion about the performance of the game itself, as well as which consoles are best to run it.

No matter which console you play GTA 6 on, Rockstar says that the game will only target 30 fps (frames per second). That's decided slow for a mainstream game in 2026. GTA 5 also shipped at 30 fps in 2013, but newer consoles can run it at higher frame rates. In fact, most games that launch on the latest generation of consoles can run at 60 fps, if not higher. While it's certainly not a dealbreaker, it is interesting that Rockstar's latest game can't run at a faster frame rate even on the PS5 Pro or the Xbox Series X.

To that point, Rockstar called out the PS5 Pro specifically in its post, announcing, "The PlayStation 5 Pro offers breathtaking visuals, with improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro."

PSSR is Sony's AI upscaler, similar to options like DLSS from Nvidia, which uses AI to add extra graphical information to games in real time. That allows developers like Rockstar to run the game at a lower resolution to save on processing power, but still boost the visuals to reach a higher perceived resolution. As such, it's not as ideal as running the game at a higher resolution natively, but it can help improve the visuals without pushing the hardware beyond its limits. Meanwhile, ray-tracing offers realistic lighting effects and can also be graphically intense.

While PlayStation and Xbox players alike will be stuck at 30 fps, it seems only PS5 Pro gamers will be able to play the game with ray-tracing effects and AI upscaling. It's surprising that Xbox Series X players don't have similar benefits, as the hardware is more powerful than Xbox Series S. Rockstar didn't specify why only the PS5 Pro gets these upgrades.

In the post, Rockstar also announced that the PS5 version of GTA 6 takes advantage of other PlayStation-exclusive perks, like high-fidelity haptic feedback in the DualSense controller, spatial audio rendering using the PlayStation's Tempest 3D audio, as well as improved load times—though Rockstar didn't specify what those load times would be. These perks apply to all PS5 consoles, not just PS5 Pros. Rockstar goes so far as to say that GTA 6 plays best on PlayStation 5 consoles.

That's not to say that Microsoft's consoles are totally left out of the perks. Rockstar says that GTA 6 will be available on Xbox Cloud Gaming on both Xbox Series X and S, as well as Xbox One. In addition, both PlayStation and Xbox gamers can play GTA 6 using Remote Play, so no one has to physically play on their console if they want to game on the go.

Again, there's no reason to go out and buy a specific console for GTA 6, so long as you have something that can run the game. After all, PS5 Pros are difficult to find, especially without wildly overpaying. But it's interesting that Rockstar has managed to give Sony's consoles the extra perks here, particularly since the company hasn't explained why that is.

#3447. Amazon's Jeff Bezos Clarifies Involvement In Robert Pattinson's James Bond Casting

As exciting as it is that Robert Pattinson has been cast as James Bond, the irony of his 007 movie being overseen by a man who is about as close to a real-life Bond villain as you're likely to get is inescapable. What does Amazon founder and chairman Jeff Bezos know about movies? Well, that remains unclear. But since Amazon bought Bond for an eye-watering sum back in 2025, he is the man who cuts the checks at the end of the day. That means he was always going to have a say in who plays Bond and it seems he was, indeed, intimately involved.

Bezos appeared at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event where he confirmed that he was "heavily involved" in Pattinson's casting (via Twitter/X). "We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on [the Friday before the official announcement was made the following Monday]," he said. "There was a big group initially, and we down-selected to five finalists."

.@JeffBezos tells @lizrhoffman he was "heavily involved" in selecting Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond.

"Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous ... but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond." pic.twitter.com/1ro4R8meYO

According to the Amazon founder, the process of whittling down the finalists (let's agree never to use the phrase "down-selected" again) involved carrying out "old-fashioned screen tests" which he described as "interesting." These tests apparently involved "full costumes and real sets and other actors," with Bezos going on to explain how each of the five candidates performed three scenes on-camera. "Then we got together on Friday to spend a couple of hours looking at all the tests and reviewing all that," he continued. "By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance. It was immediately undebated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director ... we all gravitated toward Rob."

It's interesting to hear Jeff Bezos' recollection of how Robert Pattinson was cast as James Bond. Soon after Amazon made the official announcement, reports emerged that claimed Pattinson wasn't actually director Denis Villeneuve's first choice for Bond. Instead, it seems the director was set on casting "Wake Up Dead Man" and "Disclosure Day" star Josh O'Connor, before the actor chose to take himself out of the process. To hear Bezos tell it, however, all five Bond finalists screen tested and the clear favorite was Pattinson.

Those finalists reportedly comprised O'Connor, Pattinson, "Slow Horses" star Jack Lowden, Callum Turner of the "Fantastic Beasts" films, and the man who will seemingly forever come in second to Pattinson: Nicholas Hoult. Rather than Pattinson being a second choice, in Bezos' recollection he simply came out on top after the screen tests and the decision was about as close to unanimous as you can get.

With all that in mind, it remains unclear just how the final days of the casting process unfolded. Was O'Connor still in the running on that Friday Bezos and co. watched the screen tests? How late, exactly, did Pattinson enter the process, considering he reportedly had to escape his "The Batman: Part III" contract ahead of his Bond casting? What is clear at this point is that the Amazon founder was right there alongside producers and Villeneuve to oversee the final decision.

Interestingly enough, during his Semafor event comments Jeff Bezos also claimed that Robert Pattinson didn't start out as the favorite for "Bond 26." "Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he's already so famous," he said. "Like, maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond."

Indeed, Pattinson's 007 casting breaks a 60-year tradition of casting relative unknowns as the legendary spy. As such, you can appreciate why the producers were hesitant at first. Ever since "Dr. No" launched cinema's most enduring franchise back in 1962, audiences have gotten used to seeing a fresh face in the role with each new recasting. But Pattinson's star power is actually one of the reasons he could be the best Bond yet. The last few entries in the franchise haven't been the most impressive, and the "Primetime" star will surely help restore a sense of prestige to a saga that's felt quite stale for some time. That's to say nothing of his considerable acting talent, which will no doubt immediately convince the naysayers the moment they see any footage from the film.

That certainly seems to have been the case with Bezos and the gang, who evidently felt Pattinson was a cut above the other Bond hopefuls after seeing his screen test. It remains to be seen what sort of influence the Amazon founder will have over Denis Villeneuve's movie during production, but let's hope he's too distracted by world domination to interfere too much.

#3446. Lifehacker's Pick for the Best TV to Gift in 2026 Isn't Actually a TV

Welcome to Holiday Office Hours From the Labs, a collaborative multimedia project in which Lifehacker, CNET, ZDNET, and Mashable harness the power of our product testing laboratory and our editors' expertise to offer the best gift-buying recommendations possible. In this episode, we're talking televisions.

I recently did a deep dive into TV development history, checked out what was on shelves for 2026, and I concluded that the best gift TV you can give this year is, actually, a pair of sunglasses. The XBX by XReal video display glasses are basically a TV you can shove in your pocket. Check them out:

I looked past traditional sets for a couple of reasons. First, because as much as we all love a great show or movie, who actually buys someone a TV set as a gift? More importantly, there's the nature of television itself. Since it was invented in the late 1920s, television quality has been measured by how big the screen is and how clear and bright the picture is, but in 2026, a nothing-special 4K television delivers an image that is pixel-invisible to a typical viewer, and most of us don't have living rooms big enough to need a display bigger than 65 inches. I think the innovation in the space is going to come from the form factor and the use case, and what better form factor is there than a pair of sunglasses?

These glasses deliver the equivalent of a 142" TV viewed from across the room. It's hard to compare resolution to traditional TVs—technically, the display is 1080p in each eye, but because the TV is just millimeters from your eye, it looks much clearer than that. The peak brightness is 1,600 nits, bright enough for most rooms, and there's a totally opaque shield if you need it. The refresh rate is a crisp 120Hz. They support HDR10 and real-time SDR-to-HDR upscaling, offer billions of colors, and it's all in a package that weighs only 62 grams.

Then there are the use cases. It can act as a separate monitor for your computer; you can watch a different show than your roommate without bothering them; but most of all, these are great for flights. There is no situation in life that calls for a big screen TV more than a cross-country airplane flight. Slip these on with a pair of headphones, and you can fly to Boise in your own private, virtual theater.

They plug right into any device that supports USB-C video, there's no battery to remember to charge, and they cost less than $300. In other words: They're the perfect TV gift for the holidays, even if they aren't technically a TV.

#3445. GTA 6 Officially Launches, Spoiler Warning Issued for Players Still Waiting

The global rollout of Grand Theft Auto 6 has begun

After many long years of waiting and a handful of delays, Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 will finally be released on Thursday, Nov. 19. For some players, it's out right now.

GTA 6 has a rolling midnight launch schedule, meaning it's available to play at 12 a.m. your local time on Nov. 19. Due to the power of time zones and a round Earth, midnight local time on Nov. 19 arrives in some territories while it's still Nov. 18 in others. New Zealanders will get first access as GTA 6 gradually unlocks around the world.

The internet is beholden to no time zone. Until it's midnight Nov. 19 in your time zone, you'll have to be aware that spoilers will naturally flood social media and other sites. Depending on where they live, players in New Zealand and elsewhere will have multiple hours to play GTA 6 while the timer on their PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X is still counting down. For example, midnight in New Zealand on Nov. 19 is 6 a.m. EST on Nov. 18 on the east coast of the United States. U.S.-based players will have to be careful to avoid spoilers for essentially the whole day on Wednesday.

As GTA 6 will take players a long, long time to finish, I wouldn't expect any ending spoilers to flood the internet before Nov. 19 hits your time zone. However, GTA 6 could have plenty of surprises in its early game you still might want to avoid. Need I remind you of The Last of Us Part 2's monumental opening hours?

Maybe you can't wait to play GTA 6 when it launches in your time zone and want to get your hands on it early. I get it. There is always the "New Zealand" trick you can try out, and our guide explains how to do exactly that. It's a bit more intensive for PS5 players, which make up the majority of GTA 6's massive amount of preorders.

Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on Thursday, Nov. 19. Its launch follows a fun marketing blitz that included showcasing digital dog poop on South America (formerly South Park) and taking over Miami IRL, including a crossover with the Miami Heat.

#3444. 10 Years Ago Today: Hailee Steinfeld Starred In One Of The Best Coming-Of-Age Movies Of All Time

Actor Hailee Steinfeld broke out in the Coen Brothers' 2010 Western film "True Grit" as the precocious Mattie Ross, who speaks like she's wise beyond her years but lacks the experience that brings true wisdom. We at /Film consider Steinfeld as Mattie the greatest performance in any Coens movie, which is no small feat.

Nominated for an Academy Award at only 14 years old, it would've been easy for Steinfeld's career to have peaked there. But she has kept challenging herself with music, voice acting, and plenty of new movies, and one of her best is absolutely writer/director Kelly Fremon Craig's coming-of-age film "The Edge of Seventeen."

After a premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, "The Edge of Seventeen" hit theaters on November 18, 2016. It takes its title from the Stevie Nicks song yet applies it more literally to this story about a 17-year-old girl. The acerbic, awkward, and unpopular Nadine Franklin (Steinfeld) has lost the two people in the world who understand her. One, her father, Tom (Eric Keenleyside), who died a few years prior of a heart attack. Now, her best friend, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has started dating Nadine's older brother Darian (Blake Jenner), whom Nadine loathes for having their mother Mona's (Kyra Sedgewick) favor and being so effortlessly beloved and successful.

"I've gotta spend the rest of my life with myself," Nadine says while drunk. We all realize that and then come to terms with it at some point. Nadine's story fits in the gap between the realization and the coming to terms. Speaking as someone who was the same age as Nadine was in 2016, and saw "The Edge of Seventeen" in his senior year of high school, few coming-of-age movies depict awkward adolescence in the 2010s more honestly.

Critics compared "The Edge of Seventeen" to a modern John Hughes movie, as did Hailee Steinfeld herself. In 2016, she explained to Entertainment Weekly that she hoped that the movie could reflect her generation's teen years back at them while still being timeless, in the same way "Sixteen Candles" and "The Breakfast Club" — films made for 1980s kids — still resonated with her (someone born in 1996).

But "The Edge of Seventeen" doesn't soften itself by looking to echoes of older movies instead of real life. The film begins with Nadine marching up to her history teacher, Mr. Bruner (Woody Harrelson) in his classroom, announcing she's planning to die by suicide and wants someone to know first. That opening makes you think you're in for a movie about an inspirational teacher who talks a depressed student back from the edge and shows them why life is worth living. Well, not quite.

We see, as Mr. Bruner immediately recognizes, this is Nadine being dramatic. "I don't want to take up a ton of your time" she says right off, which is her first lie. The movie then rewinds (with the help of some voiceover from Nadine, though that fades pretty quickly) before catching back up with this cold open. What led to her current situation? Nadine accidentally sent a text to her crush, Nick (Alexander Calvert), describing very explicitly how she wants to hook up with him.

That complements one of the best bits of writing in the film, one that definitely helped it speak to my younger self. Nadine has a lot of movie-typical teenage boy qualities: she doesn't fit in, dresses in baggy sweatshirts, has a hopeless crush she never talks to, makes sex jokes while mistaking vulgarity for wit, etc.

During the "Edge of Seventeen" press tour, Kelly Fremon Craig and producer James L. Brooks spoke with /Film. Craig cited some "life-altering" writing advice from Brooks, that she needed to ask herself, "What is this movie saying about life?" I would answer that "The Edge of Seventeen" is about how, when you're a teenager, your problems seem like the whole world and that part of growing up is realizing others — even people who irritate you everyday (as Nadine's mom and brother do to her) — are dealing with their own pain.

Upon its release, "The Edge of Seventeen" saw only modest financial success, grossing $19 million in theaters against its $9 million budget. A spin-off TV series ordered by YouTube Red ultimately didn't move forward, either. I would also argue the film's anticipated reputation as "definitive teen movie of the 2010s" was overshadowed by Greta Gerwig's "Lady Bird," which came out the following year and hits similar beats while finding both great financial success and critical acclaim. Not that "The Edge of Seventeen" has been lost to time or anything, though.

In that aforementioned /Film interview, Craig claimed, "If [Hailee Steinfeld] didn't exist, the movie wouldn't exist," because she brought a sui generis quality to Nadine as she once did to Mattie Ross. The two would work together again on the "Transformers" spin-off film "Bumblebee," where Steinfeld starred and Craig performed rewrites. "Bumblebee" often feels like "The Edge of Seventeen" but with Transformers included.

A couple of times in "The Edge of Seventeen," Nadine looks up to the sky and asks if God is even paying attention to her. Perhaps it's not surprising that when Craig directed another coming-of-age film, she adapted Judy Blume's classic novel "Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret."

#3443. GTA 6: How Long Until You Can Play As Lucia

While Grand Theft Auto 5 had you juggle three people through a campaign, GTA 6 saddles you with a couple: Jason and Lucia. Although some fans will miss the hectic nature of three hotheads, Jason and Lucia bring a completely different vibe to GTA, and can go on missions together.

Initially, you'll start the game as Jason, with Lucia currently serving time in Leonida Penitentiary. Eventually, the two will cross paths, and you can play the game with both protagonists. Here's how long you'll need to wait until Lucia not only enters the picture, but is fully absorbed into the story.

Spoiling as little as possible, you'll get a short intro scene as Lucia in Leonida Penitentiary, then the perspective will immediately shift to Jason for quite some time. After progressing through the campaign a bit, Lucia will eventually start a work release program and will be allowed to return home and reunite with Jason.

The thing is, it will take some time until Lucia is actually brought on board. The opening hours of the game are firmly rooted in Jason's story, with periodic updates on Lucia's situation, bookended by phone calls about plans for when she gets out.

To be clear, here are my stats, which you can cross-reference with your own on the "progress" pause menu:

Since story completion is the same for everyone, this is one of the most accurate stats for when Lucia joins the game in earnest. The time it takes to get to this point varies (since you don't always need to progress with the campaign), but the percentage of story completion is a good barometer for where you're at.

The ability to freely swap between characters arrives later in the game, in Chapter 2 (I hit this around the 15-hour mark). You'll take full control of Lucia for a while, eventually coming across a mission called "Breakfast Run." This core mission will teach you how to use the "protagonist swapping" mechanic from GTA 5, and will then let players swap between Jason and Lucia freely for most of the game (minus some mission-specific circumstances).

To do this, hold down the right D-pad button to swap between Jason and Lucia with L1 and R1. Alternatively, you can also invite Jason or Lucia along on most events, including side missions or roaming around the open world causing havoc. If there's a restriction, the game will let you know in advance, like "Jason Only" or "Lucia Only" for specific story missions.

For the most part, story missions will bring Jason and Lucia into the fold automatically, so there's no reason to have to micromanage where any character is at any time. In GTA 6, quality of life and convenience are at the forefront, and you can even choose to play mostly as one character if you want.

#3442. The Rings Of Power Season 3's Best Storyline Redeems A Controversial Peter Jackson Idea

Spoilers are never late (nor are they early; they arrive precisely when they mean to), so don't read ahead without first watching Season 3, Episodes 5 and 6 of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power."

Over halfway into its run, it's clear "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3 is spectacular whenever Sauron (Charlie Vickers) is on-screen. Indeed, this season is for the baddies, with the Dark Lord's menacing Nazgnagôl making their grand entrance and a thrilling civil war brewing in Númenor.

But it's not all doom and gloom, as Season 3 also introduces the brightest light of hope in Middle-earth: the elven golden retriver Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). From the moment he shows up, it feels like he's been a part of the show from the start, fitting in perfectly as a strong, funny, flirty elf who has excellent chemistry with Galadriel (Morfydd Clark). Celeborn is the ultimate wife guy, and his relationship with Galadriel is the best romance we've seen in a Middle-earth adventure to date.

Nevertheless, there's trouble in Valinor for these two, as Celeborn has competition for Galadriel's heart. No, not Robert Aramayo's Elrond (despite them sharing a kiss in Season 2 to distract the orcs holding Galadriel captive), but Sauron, the Dark Lord on his dark throne in the Land of Mordor where the Shadows lie.

That's right: "The Rings of Power" Season 3 has finally turned "The Lord of the Rings" into a romantasy story, placing a love triangle at the heart of the saga of the One Ring. And while J.R.R. Tolkien purists may scoff at this, the show's love triangle is so good that it redeems the controversial romances from Peter Jackson's otherwise beloved "Lord of the Rings" films.

Peter Jackson's "Lord of the Rings" films are the most widely celebrated fantasy movies of all time and changed the genre forever. As such, it's easy nowadays to forget that Jackson's trilogy stirred up its fair share of controversy upon its initial release. After all, as faithful as they were to J.R.R. Tolkien's original books overall, those films also made some big alterations. That includes erasing the Scouring of The Shire from "The Return of the King" and removing characters like Tom Bombadil and Glorfindel, in addition to introducing a prominent love triangle.

In Jackson's movies, to jog your memory, a respectable amount of time is spent on Éowyn (Miranda Otto) falling in love with Aragorn (Viggo Mortensen), with even King Théoden (Bernard Hill) buying into their match and congratulating Éowyn on finding a good and honest man. Meanwhile, Aragorn keeps thinking about Arwen (Liv Tyler), who is about to leave Middle-earth for Valinor. In fact, the original plan was for Arwen to be at Helm's Deep alongside Éowyn and Aragorn in "The Two Towers," which presumably would've fueled their love triangle even further.

Things get even worse in Jackson's "The Hobbit" films. There, he and co-writers Philippa Boyens and Fran Walsh introduce Tauriel (Evangeline Lilly), an elf who develops romantic feelings for the dwarf Kili (Aidan Turner). In that case, it's Legolas (Orlando Bloom) who rounds out the love triangle, as he's still racist towards dwarves at the time.

Neither of these Middle-earth love triangles really work (especially not the latter), so it's hard not to be skeptical of "The Rings of Power" introducing yet another one. And yet, this ends up being the most compelling aspect of Season 3.

There are two things that make the love triangle in "The Rings of Power" work. The first is that the show is very clearly in on the joke, with Sauron often behaving like a teenager when it comes to his borderline hilarious fixation on Galadriel. That he even goes to the trouble of disguising himself as Galadriel and kissing Celeborn to get information out of him shows Sauron is not beyond being a little bi-curious.

Then there's the fact that the series has been building to this since Season 1, starting with Galadriel slowly falling for Sauron in disguise as Halbrand and being seduced by his promises of power. By the time Season 3 rolls along, she still has complicated feelings for him, as evidenced by her dreams and visions of Sauron waking up in bed next to her. Thus, when Celeborn re-enters her life, and Galadriel sees both men in front of her, there's a tiny bit of hesitation on her part.

And yet, Season 3 never suggests that Galadriel would actually leave her husband for the Dark Lord. Instead, it juxtaposes Sauron's jealousy with Celeborn's confidence. Specifically, in Episodes 5 and 6, Sauron gets visibly flustered when Celeborn talks about how much Galadriel loves him. In the end, it works just as well as the incredible romances in J.R.R. Tolkien's source material, proving that Middle-earth is not devoid of effective romantic storytelling.

Heck, the scene in Episode 6where Celeborn talks about making the elven smith that Sauron has been looking for tell him the secrets of the rings, just so he can hear about every minute the smith spent with Galadriel, is arguably the most romantic TV scene of 2026. Stream Season 3 on Prime Video, and see for yourself.

#3441. 20 Years Later, Paramount's Serial Killer Series Officially Breaks a Weird TV Record

The Last of Us star talks about getting into the mindset of a serial killer and why filming Dexter made him feel "like a baby bird"

The Last of Us star talks about getting into the mindset of a serial killer and why filming Dexter made him feel "like a baby bird"

Gabriel Luna has a rule: He doesn't play villains unless it's opposite "the greatest action hero who's ever lived," aka Arnold Schwarzenegger. "I have an I only play heroes kind of mindset," the actor tells Polygon.

This isn't just an aspirational goal. It's already happened twice. Luna portrayed Rev-9, an advanced killer robot in Terminator: Dark Fate, and he was an evil arms dealer in the Netflix series FUBAR, both of which starred Schwarzenegger. But in 2026, Luna broke his own rule to take on a very different kind of role: a serial killer.

Luna plays Ray Ballard, aka the Sleepy-Eyed Killer, across two episodes of Dexter: Resurrection season 2. It's a role he was drawn to because of the complex psychology at work within the character, who stalks and kills his victims while they sleep.

"I was fascinated by the psychological warfare he plays with them as he does these home invasions and enters the home for weeks and weeks before he ever culminates the kill," Luna says.

Speaking to Polygon, the Last of Us star goes deep into the backstory he invented for the Sleepy-Eyed Killer and the surprising record he broke while shooting his most pivotal scene.

Spoilers follow for Dexter: Resurrection season 2 episode 3.

Luna does have some experience with serial killers. He played real-life detective Rafael Tovar in the 2025 miniseries Devil in Disguise: John Wayne Gacy, where he helped track down the infamous murderer. Luna learned a lot about what makes someone become a serial killer while working on the show; specifically, that many serial killers tend to have experienced a childhood trauma of their own.

The actor took that lesson and applied it to Ray Ballard as an explanation for why he kills.

"It's mostly about freeing these people from the binds that they have to family, to other human beings in general," he says. "They can only serve to hurt you."

"That's something that was probably beaten into him. Some kind of heinous abuse he endured early in his life, which is often the case. This guy was definitely messed up somewhere in his childhood. The people who were closest to him abandoned and abused him. He was never able to shake that and forgive that, and now he's taken it out on everyone."

Like so many serial killers before him, Ballard ultimately winds up on Dexter Morgan's operating table where Michael C. Hall's anti-hero delivers his own unique brand of vigilante justice by tying them down under sheets of plastic wrap, reminding them of their terrible crimes, and then murdering them in cold blood.

Plenty of great actors, from John Lithgow to Neil Patrick Harris, have met the same fate on Dexter. However, Luna's death scene appears to have broken a very specific record.

"I may have set a record for most time on the table, which I'm very proud of," Luna says, citing the show's executive producer, Scott Reynolds, as his source.

"That scene was a bit long. It starts with a whole scene between Michael and Uma [Thurman], and then it transitions into a scene between Michael and I. And so I spent a lot of time on the table that day. I don't know what they clocked it at, but apparently it was a record."

You're completely strapped to the table, and they have a little sippy cup with juice for you and feed you Cheerios or whatever you wanna eat and just hand it like a baby bird.

Records aside, Luna seemingly had a blast being murdered onscreen in a scene that involves Dexter driving an ice pick (Ballard's murder weapon of choice) right into the serial killer's forehead.

"It's such an iconic place to be," Luna says. "Many greats have been on that table and have felt the point of Dexter's knife."

"You can't move, and your arms are bound to your sides. You're completely strapped to the table, and they have a little sippy cup with juice for you and feed you Cheerios or whatever you wanna eat and just hand it like a baby bird."

That doesn't exactly sound like fun, but maybe Luna is just built different. Then again, it probably helped that his wife was also there to keep him company in between takes.

"My wife, who's a massive fan of the show and has always been, was on set that day," Luna says. "We have a great photograph of her standing over me as I'm bound, completely wrapped in Saran Wrap. I've joked that she could ask me for anything in that moment, and I would've been powerless against her."

Dexter: Resurrection is streaming now on Paramount Plus.
